§0Before you start

The big picture

Course III answers two questions. How do we fit a linear model when the output is a class rather than a number? And how do we minimize the resulting average loss when the dataset is too large to look at all of it at every step?

The whole lecture revolves around one kind of objective, an average of per-example losses:

The finite-sum objective

min⁡β F(β)=1n∑i=1nℓi(β),ℓi(β)=loss of the model β on example (xi,yi).\displaystyle {\min_{\bbeta}\ F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\bbeta),}\qquad\allowbreak \ell_i(\bbeta)=\text{loss of the model }\bbeta\text{ on example }(\bx_i,y_i).βmin​ F(β)=n1​i=1∑n​ℓi​(β),ℓi​(β)=loss of the model β on example (xi​,yi​).
  • Part 1, linear classification (§1–§5), decides which ℓi\ell_iℓi​ to use. The linear score xi⊤β\bx_i\T\bbetaxi⊤​β is turned into a class (its sign), the quality of a prediction is summarized by the margin yixi⊤βy_i\bx_i\T\bbetayi​xi⊤​β, the unusable 0–1 loss is replaced by the smooth convex logistic loss, which turns out to be the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model. With KKK classes the same reasoning gives the softmax and the cross-entropy.
  • Part 2, stochastic optimization (§6–§13), decides how to minimize FFF when nnn is large. Gradient descent touches all nnn examples per step; stochastic gradient descent uses one (or a few) and pays with noise. The rest of the lecture is about controlling that noise: mini-batches, learning-rate schedules, momentum, adaptive step sizes (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam) and variance reduction (SAG, SAGA, SVRG).

Probability and optimization toolkit Beyond the slides

Bernoulli and categorical distributions, likelihood

A Bernoulli variable takes the value 1 with probability π\piπ and 0 with probability 1−π1-\pi1−π; compactly P(Y=y)=πy(1−π)1−yP(Y=y)=\pi^y(1-\pi)^{1-y}P(Y=y)=πy(1−π)1−y for y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1}. A categorical variable takes value k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}k∈{1,…,K} with probability pkp_kpk​; with the one-hot vector y\byy, P(Y=k)=∏j=1KpjyjP(Y=k)=\prod_{j=1}^Kp_j^{y_j}P(Y=k)=∏j=1K​pjyj​​. For independent observations the likelihood is the product of these probabilities, so the log-likelihood is a sum, and maximizing it is minimizing the negative log-likelihood −∑ilog⁡P(yi∣xi)-\sum_i\log P(y_i\mid\bx_i)−∑i​logP(yi​∣xi​): exactly a finite sum.

Smoothness and strong convexity

FFF is LLL-smooth if ∥∇F(β)−∇F(β′)∥≤L∥β−β′∥\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta)-\nabla F(\bbeta')}\le L\norm{\bbeta-\bbeta'}​∇F(β)−∇F(β′)​≤L​β−β′​; for a twice differentiable convex FFF this means ∇2F⪯LI\nabla^2F\preceq L\bI∇2F⪯LI (in general, −LI⪯∇2F⪯LI-L\bI\preceq\nabla^2F\preceq L\bI−LI⪯∇2F⪯LI). It implies the descent lemma F(β′)≤F(β)+∇F(β)⊤(β′−β)+L2∥β′−β∥2F(\bbeta')\le F(\bbeta)+\nabla F(\bbeta)\T(\bbeta'-\bbeta)+\frac L2\norm{\bbeta'-\bbeta}^2F(β′)≤F(β)+∇F(β)⊤(β′−β)+2L​​β′−β​2. FFF is μ\muμ-strongly convex if ∇2F⪰μI\nabla^2F\succeq\mu\bI∇2F⪰μI with μ>0\mu>0μ>0; then it has a unique minimizer β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ and ⟨∇F(β),β−β⋆⟩≥μ∥β−β⋆∥2\langle\nabla F(\bbeta),\bbeta-\bbeta^\star\rangle\ge\mu\norm{\bbeta-\bbeta^\star}^2⟨∇F(β),β−β⋆⟩≥μ∥β−β⋆∥2. The ratio κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\muκ=L/μ is the condition number of the problem.

Conditional expectation and unbiased estimators

In SGD the randomness comes only from which examples we pick. "Conditionally on β(t)\bbeta^{(t)}β(t)" means: the current iterate is fixed, and we average over the random index. The tower rule E[E[Z∣β(t)]]=E[Z]\E[\E[Z\mid\bbeta^{(t)}]]=\E[Z]E[E[Z∣β(t)]]=E[Z] then lets us chain one-step statements over many steps. An estimator is unbiased if its expectation is the target. For bbb draws with replacement, the variance of an average is the single-draw variance divided by bbb.

Exponential moving averages

The recursion at=θat−1+(1−θ)zta_t=\theta a_{t-1}+(1-\theta)z_tat​=θat−1​+(1−θ)zt​ with a0=0a_0=0a0​=0 unrolls to at=(1−θ)∑k=1tθt−kzka_t=(1-\theta)\sum_{k=1}^t\theta^{t-k}z_kat​=(1−θ)∑k=1t​θt−kzk​: a weighted average of the past with geometrically decaying weights. Its memory is about 1/(1−θ)1/(1-\theta)1/(1−θ) steps (10 for θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9, 1000 for θ=0.999\theta=0.999θ=0.999). Because it starts at 0, the weights sum to 1−θt1-\theta^t1−θt rather than 1, so early values are biased toward zero. This is the reason for Adam's bias correction (§12).

Series

∑t≥1t−p\sum_{t\ge1}t^{-p}∑t≥1​t−p converges if and only if p>1p>1p>1 (integral test). So ∑1/t=∞\sum1/t=\infty∑1/t=∞ (harmonic series) while ∑1/t2=π2/6\sum1/t^2=\pi^2/6∑1/t2=π2/6. This single fact decides which power-law learning-rate schedules satisfy the classical convergence conditions (§10).

§1Slides pp. 2–4

From regression to classification

Keep the linear model of Course II, but read its output as a score: its sign gives the class, and the set where it vanishes is a straight line, a plane, or a hyperplane that separates the two classes.

Scores and the sign rule

In regression (Course II), yi∈Ry_i\in\Ryi​∈R and fβ(xi)=xi⊤βf_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)=\bx_i\T\bbetafβ​(xi​)=xi⊤​β predicts the real-valued output directly. In binary classification the output is a label,

yi∈{−1,+1},\displaystyle y_i\in\{-1,+1\},yi​∈{−1,+1},

and the linear model is reinterpreted as a score fβ(x)=x⊤βf_{\bbeta}(\bx)=\bx\T\bbetafβ​(x)=x⊤β. As in Course II, x\bxx is the augmented vector [1,x1,…,xd]⊤[1,x_1,\dots,x_d]\T[1,x1​,…,xd​]⊤, so the intercept is the first entry of β\bbetaβ. The predicted class is the sign of the score:

Slide p. 3 · prediction

y^=sign⁡(fβ(x)).\displaystyle \widehat y=\sign\big(f_{\bbeta}(\bx)\big).y​=sign(fβ​(x)).

Coding the classes as −1-1−1 and +1+1+1 is a convenience, not a necessity. It makes the sign of the score the prediction and, in §2, makes the product y fβ(x)y\,f_{\bbeta}(\bx)yfβ​(x) positive exactly when the prediction is right. Section 3 switches to the {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1} coding when probabilities are more natural; nothing changes except bookkeeping.

The decision boundary is a hyperplane

The classifier changes its answer where the score changes sign, so the decision boundary is

Slide p. 4

{x: x⊤β=0}={x: β0+w⊤x1:d=0},w=β1:d.\displaystyle {\{\bx:\ \bx\T\bbeta=0\}}=\allowbreak{\{\bx:\ \beta_0+\bw\T\bx_{1:d}=0\}},\qquad\allowbreak { \bw=\bbeta_{1:d}.}{x: x⊤β=0}={x: β0​+w⊤x1:d​=0},w=β1:d​.

In two dimensions this is a straight line, in three a plane, in general a hyperplane: a flat set of dimension d−1d-1d−1 that cuts the feature space into two half-spaces, {fβ>0}\{f_{\bbeta}>0\}{fβ​>0} (predict +1+1+1) and {fβ<0}\{f_{\bbeta}<0\}{fβ​<0} (predict −1-1−1). A linear classifier can only produce such a split; anything curved requires basis functions (Course II, §1).

What the magnitude of the score means

The slide adds that ∣fβ(x)∣\abs{f_{\bbeta}(\bx)}∣fβ​(x)∣ "measures the signed separation from the decision boundary". Precisely:

dist(x,boundary)=∣fβ(x)∣∥w∥2,signed distance=fβ(x)∥w∥2.\displaystyle \mathrm{dist}(\bx,\text{boundary})=\frac{\abs{f_{\bbeta}(\bx)}}{\norm{\bw}_2},\qquad\allowbreak { \text{signed distance}=\frac{f_{\bbeta}(\bx)}{\norm{\bw}_2}.}dist(x,boundary)=∥w∥2​∣fβ​(x)∣​,signed distance=∥w∥2​fβ​(x)​.

Derivation

  1. Writing z=x1:d\bz=\bx_{1:d}z=x1:d​ for the raw features, the boundary is {z:w⊤z+β0=0}\{\bz:\bw\T\bz+\beta_0=0\}{z:w⊤z+β0​=0}. If z0\bz_0z0​ and z1\bz_1z1​ are both on it, w⊤(z1−z0)=0\bw\T(\bz_1-\bz_0)=0w⊤(z1​−z0​)=0: every direction inside the boundary is orthogonal to w\bww. So w\bww is the normal vector of the hyperplane.
  2. The distance from a point z\bzz to the hyperplane is the length of the projection of z−z0\bz-\bz_0z−z0​ onto the unit normal w/∥w∥\bw/\norm{\bw}w/∥w∥, for any z0\bz_0z0​ on the boundary: w⊤(z−z0)∥w∥=w⊤z−w⊤z0∥w∥=w⊤z+β0∥w∥\frac{\bw\T(\bz-\bz_0)}{\norm{\bw}}=\frac{\bw\T\bz-\bw\T\bz_0}{\norm{\bw}}=\frac{\bw\T\bz+\beta_0}{\norm{\bw}}∥w∥w⊤(z−z0​)​=∥w∥w⊤z−w⊤z0​​=∥w∥w⊤z+β0​​, using w⊤z0=−β0\bw\T\bz_0=-\beta_0w⊤z0​=−β0​.
  3. The numerator is the score fβ(x)f_{\bbeta}(\bx)fβ​(x). Its sign says on which side of the boundary z\bzz lies.
∎

So the score is the distance to the boundary, measured in units of 1/∥w∥1/\norm{\bw}1/∥w∥. Multiplying β\bbetaβ by any c>0c>0c>0 leaves the boundary and every prediction unchanged but multiplies every score by ccc: the direction of β\bbetaβ decides the classifier, its length decides how large (how "confident") the scores are. Keep this scale freedom in mind; it explains why logistic regression can run off to infinity on separable data (§4).

Why not just use least squares on the labels? Beyond the slides

One could fit x⊤β≈y\bx\T\bbeta\approx yx⊤β≈y by least squares with y∈{−1,+1}y\in\{-1,+1\}y∈{−1,+1} and then take the sign. It works poorly, and the reason motivates §2. The squared error (y−x⊤β)2(y-\bx\T\bbeta)^2(y−x⊤β)2 is large not only when the score has the wrong sign but also when it has the right sign and is "too large": a point with y=+1y=+1y=+1 and score 333 costs (1−3)2=4(1-3)^2=4(1−3)2=4, more than a misclassified point with score −0.5-0.5−0.5 (cost 2.252.252.25). Points far on the correct side therefore drag the boundary toward themselves. A classification loss should only care about the sign of y x⊤βy\,\bx\T\bbetayx⊤β and about how confidently it is right, which is exactly what the margin captures.

Check yourself

1.1The classifier β=(1,−1,2)\bbeta=(1,-1,2)β=(1,−1,2) scores the point (x1,x2)=(3,1)(x_1,x_2)=(3,1)(x1​,x2​)=(3,1). What is the prediction, and how far is the point from the boundary?

f=1−3+2=0f=1-3+2=0f=1−3+2=0: the point lies exactly on the boundary, distance 0, and the sign rule cannot decide (by convention one picks a class, or reports a tie).

1.2Why is w=β1:d\bw=\bbeta_{1:d}w=β1:d​ orthogonal to the decision boundary?

For two points z0,z1\bz_0,\bz_1z0​,z1​ on the boundary, w⊤z0=w⊤z1=−β0\bw\T\bz_0=\bw\T\bz_1=-\beta_0w⊤z0​=w⊤z1​=−β0​, so w⊤(z1−z0)=0\bw\T(\bz_1-\bz_0)=0w⊤(z1​−z0​)=0: w\bww is orthogonal to every direction lying in the boundary.

1.3You replace β\bbetaβ by 10 β10\,\bbeta10β. What changes?

Nothing about the classifier: same boundary, same predictions, same distances. Every score is multiplied by 10. Losses that depend on the size of the score (logistic, §3) do change.

§2Slides pp. 5–7

How should we train a classifier? Margins and the 0–1 loss

Multiply the label by the score and you get one number per example that says both whether the prediction is right and how confidently. Every classification loss in this course is a function of that number.

The margin

Slide p. 5

mi=yi fβ(xi)=yi xi⊤β.\displaystyle m_i=y_i\,f_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)=y_i\,\bx_i\T\bbeta.mi​=yi​fβ​(xi​)=yi​xi⊤​β.

Because yi∈{−1,+1}y_i\in\{-1,+1\}yi​∈{−1,+1}, multiplying by yiy_iyi​ flips the score for negative examples, so that "good" always means "positive":

Slide p. 6

mi>0⟺correct classification,mi<0⟹misclassified observation.\displaystyle {m_i>0}\quad\allowbreak {\Longleftrightarrow}\quad\allowbreak {\text{correct classification},}\qquad\allowbreak { m_i<0}\quad\allowbreak {\Longrightarrow}\quad\allowbreak {\text{misclassified observation}.}mi​>0⟺correct classification,mi​<0⟹misclassified observation.

Derivation

The prediction is correct when sign⁡(fβ(xi))=yi\sign(f_{\bbeta}(\bx_i))=y_isign(fβ​(xi​))=yi​. If yi=+1y_i=+1yi​=+1 this means fβ(xi)>0f_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)>0fβ​(xi​)>0, i.e. mi=fβ(xi)>0m_i=f_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)>0mi​=fβ​(xi​)>0. If yi=−1y_i=-1yi​=−1 it means fβ(xi)<0f_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)<0fβ​(xi​)<0, i.e. mi=−fβ(xi)>0m_i=-f_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)>0mi​=−fβ​(xi​)>0. In both cases: correct   ⟺  mi>0\iff m_i>0⟺mi​>0.

∎

The size matters too: a large positive margin indicates a confidently classified observation, one that sits far inside the correct half-space. By §1, mi/∥w∥m_i/\norm{\bw}mi​/∥w∥ is the signed distance of xi\bx_ixi​ to the boundary, positive on the correct side (the geometric margin). Support vector machines are built on that quantity.

Intuition

Think of the margin as a "correctness score" for each example. Strongly negative: the model is confidently wrong. Around zero: the example sits near the boundary and a small change of β\bbetaβ flips it. Strongly positive: safely classified. A good classifier pushes all margins to the right. A good loss is therefore a decreasing function of the margin.

The ideal loss and why we cannot use it

What we really care about is the number of mistakes. The 0–1 loss counts them:

Slide p. 7

ℓ0/1(m)=1{m≤0},1n∑i=1nℓ0/1(mi)=training error rate.\displaystyle {\lzo(m)=\ind_{\{m\le0\}},}\qquad\allowbreak { \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\lzo(m_i)=\text{training error rate}.}ℓ0/1​(m)=1{m≤0}​,n1​i=1∑n​ℓ0/1​(mi​)=training error rate.

(A point exactly on the boundary, mi=0m_i=0mi​=0, counts as an error.) Minimizing this directly is hopeless, because the loss is

discontinuous and nonconvex.\displaystyle \text{discontinuous and nonconvex.}discontinuous and nonconvex.
  • No gradient information. As a function of β\bbetaβ, the error rate is piecewise constant: its gradient is zero wherever it exists. Gradient descent has nothing to follow.
  • Jumps. An infinitesimal change of β\bbetaβ can move a point across the boundary and change the objective by 1/n1/n1/n.
  • Nonconvex and combinatorial. Many separate flat regions, many local minima. Finding the hyperplane with the fewest training errors is NP-hard in general when the classes are not perfectly separable.

Convex surrogates

The fix is to replace ℓ0/1\lzoℓ0/1​ by a surrogate ϕ(m)\phi(m)ϕ(m) that is convex and decreasing in the margin, and as smooth as possible. Since mi=yixi⊤βm_i=y_i\bx_i\T\bbetami​=yi​xi⊤​β is linear in β\bbetaβ, each ϕ(mi(β))\phi(m_i(\bbeta))ϕ(mi​(β)) is a convex function of β\bbetaβ (a convex function of an affine map), and so is the average F(β)=1n∑iϕ(mi)F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_i\phi(m_i)F(β)=n1​∑i​ϕ(mi​). The non-convex counting problem becomes a convex optimization problem.

The squared row explains the remark at the end of §1: for y∈{±1}y\in\{\pm1\}y∈{±1}, (y−f)2=(1−yf)2(y-f)^2=(1-yf)^2(y−f)2=(1−yf)2 because y2=1y^2=1y2=1, so least squares on the labels is exactly the squared margin loss, which charges correct but confident predictions. Note also that with the natural logarithm the logistic loss equals log⁡2≈0.69\log2\approx0.69log2≈0.69 at m=0m=0m=0; dividing it by log⁡2\log2log2 (logarithm in base 2) turns it into an upper bound on the 0–1 loss, so its average bounds the training error rate.

The slides single out the logistic loss: a smooth convex surrogate is the logistic loss; it also has a probabilistic interpretation, the subject of §3.

2.1An example has y=−1y=-1y=−1 and score 0.30.30.3. What is its margin, and is it classified correctly?

m=−0.3<0m=-0.3<0m=−0.3<0: misclassified, but only barely (it is close to the boundary).

2.2Why can't gradient descent minimize the training error rate directly?

As a function of β\bbetaβ the error rate is piecewise constant: its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jumps, so gradient steps never move.

2.3Show that least squares on labels y∈{−1,+1}y\in\{-1,+1\}y∈{−1,+1} uses the loss (1−m)2(1-m)^2(1−m)2, and explain the problem.

(y−f)2=y2(1−f/y)2=(1−yf)2(y-f)^2=y^2(1-f/y)^2=(1-yf)^2(y−f)2=y2(1−f/y)2=(1−yf)2 since y2=1y^2=1y2=1 and 1/y=y1/y=y1/y=y. The function (1−m)2(1-m)^2(1−m)2 increases for m>1m>1m>1, so correctly classified points with large margins are penalized and pull the boundary toward them.

2.4Why is F(β)=1n∑iϕ(yixi⊤β)F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_i\phi(y_i\bx_i\T\bbeta)F(β)=n1​∑i​ϕ(yi​xi⊤​β) convex whenever ϕ\phiϕ is convex?

Each margin is an affine (here linear) function of β\bbetaβ, a convex function composed with an affine map is convex, and an average of convex functions is convex.

§3Slides pp. 8–13

The logistic loss and the Bernoulli model

The logistic loss is not an arbitrary smooth surrogate: pass the score through the sigmoid to get a probability, model the label as a Bernoulli draw, and the negative log-likelihood is exactly the logistic loss of the margin.

Logistic regression as a Bernoulli model

Temporarily code the labels as Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\}Y∈{0,1}. Logistic regression assumes that, given the input, the label is a biased coin flip whose bias is the sigmoid of the linear score:

Slide p. 12

Y∣X=x ∼ Bernoulli⁡(πβ(x)),πβ(x)=σ(fβ(x)).\displaystyle {Y\mid X=\bx\ \sim\ \Ber\big(\pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)\big),}\qquad\allowbreak { \pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)=\sigma\big(f_{\bbeta}(\bx)\big).}Y∣X=x ∼ Bernoulli(πβ​(x)),πβ​(x)=σ(fβ​(x)).

Thus Pβ(Y=1∣X=x)=πβ(x)P_{\bbeta}(Y=1\mid X=\bx)=\pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)Pβ​(Y=1∣X=x)=πβ​(x) and Pβ(Y=0∣X=x)=1−πβ(x)P_{\bbeta}(Y=0\mid X=\bx)=1-\pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)Pβ​(Y=0∣X=x)=1−πβ​(x).

What the coefficients mean. Inverting the sigmoid, the model says that the log-odds are linear in the features:

log⁡P(Y=1∣x)P(Y=0∣x)=logit⁡(πβ(x))=x⊤β=β0+β1x1+⋯+βdxd.\displaystyle \log\frac{P(Y=1\mid\bx)}{P(Y=0\mid\bx)}=\logit\big(\pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)\big)=\bx\T\bbeta=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots+\beta_dx_d.logP(Y=0∣x)P(Y=1∣x)​=logit(πβ​(x))=x⊤β=β0​+β1​x1​+⋯+βd​xd​.

Increasing xjx_jxj​ by one unit adds βj\beta_jβj​ to the log-odds, i.e. multiplies the odds by eβje^{\beta_j}eβj​ (the odds ratio). This is how logistic regression coefficients are reported in medicine and the social sciences.

Now take minus the logarithm, using −log⁡σ(u)=log⁡(1+e−u)-\log\sigma(u)=\log(1+e^{-u})−logσ(u)=log(1+e−u):

−log⁡pβ(yi∣xi)=log⁡(1+exp⁡[−yifβ(xi)])=ℓlog⁡(yifβ(xi))=ℓlog⁡(mi).\displaystyle -\log p_{\bbeta}(y_i\mid\bx_i)=\log\big(1+\exp[-y_if_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)]\big)=\llog\big(y_if_{\bbeta}(\bx_i)\big)=\llog(m_i).−logpβ​(yi​∣xi​)=log(1+exp[−yi​fβ​(xi​)])=ℓlog​(yi​fβ​(xi​))=ℓlog​(mi​).

Logistic loss = Bernoulli negative log-likelihood.

The probability that the model assigns to the observed label is σ(mi)\sigma(m_i)σ(mi​): a large positive margin means the model gave the true label a probability close to 1, a large negative margin means it gave it almost none. The loss −log⁡σ(mi)-\log\sigma(m_i)−logσ(mi​) measures the "surprise".

From one example to the dataset

For independent examples the likelihood is ∏ipβ(yi∣xi)\prod_ip_{\bbeta}(y_i\mid\bx_i)∏i​pβ​(yi​∣xi​); its negative logarithm divided by nnn is 1n∑iℓlog⁡(mi)\frac1n\sum_i\llog(m_i)n1​∑i​ℓlog​(mi​). Maximum likelihood estimation of logistic regression is the minimization of the average logistic loss. That finite-sum problem is the subject of §4.

From probabilities to decisions Beyond the slides

Predicting the more likely class means y^=1\widehat y=1y​=1 when πβ(x)>12\pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)>\tfrac12πβ​(x)>21​, i.e. when x⊤β>0\bx\T\bbeta>0x⊤β>0: the sign rule of §1. When the two kinds of error have different costs (missing a disease is worse than a false alarm), one predicts 111 when πβ(x)>t\pi_{\bbeta}(\bx)>tπβ​(x)>t for some threshold ttt, equivalently when x⊤β>logit⁡(t)\bx\T\bbeta>\logit(t)x⊤β>logit(t). The boundary moves parallel to itself; the model does not need to be refitted.

§4Slide p. 14

Optimizing logistic regression

Maximum likelihood is a smooth convex finite-sum problem with a simple gradient, a curvature bounded by one quarter, and no closed-form solution. Gradient descent solves it; Newton's method turns out to be the IRLS algorithm of Course II.

The objective

Maximum likelihood amounts to minimizing the finite-sum objective

Slide p. 14

F(β)=1n∑i=1nℓi(β),ℓi(β)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−yixi⊤β)).\displaystyle {F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\bbeta),}\qquad\allowbreak { \ell_i(\bbeta)=\log\big(1+\exp(-y_i\bx_i\T\bbeta)\big).}F(β)=n1​i=1∑n​ℓi​(β),ℓi​(β)=log(1+exp(−yi​xi⊤​β)).

Each term is the logistic loss of one margin, so FFF is convex (§2). The 1n\frac1nn1​ makes FFF an average rather than a sum, which keeps its scale independent of nnn and will make "pick one term at random" an unbiased estimate in §7.

The gradient

In matrix form, with m=y⊙(Xβ)\mathbf{m}=\by\odot(\bX\bbeta)m=y⊙(Xβ) the vector of margins, ∇F(β)=−1nX⊤(y⊙σ(−m))\nabla F(\bbeta)=-\frac1n\bX\T\big(\by\odot\sigma(-\mathbf{m})\big)∇F(β)=−n1​X⊤(y⊙σ(−m)): one product with X\bXX to get the margins, one with X⊤\bX\TX⊤ to get the gradient, O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) operations.

Intuition · reading the gradient

A gradient step β←β−γ∇ℓi\bbeta\leftarrow\bbeta-\gamma\nabla\ell_iβ←β−γ∇ℓi​ adds γ σ(−mi) yixi\gamma\,\sigma(-m_i)\,y_i\bx_iγσ(−mi​)yi​xi​ to β\bbetaβ: it moves the boundary so as to increase the margin of example iii. The weight σ(−mi)=1−pβ(yi∣xi)\sigma(-m_i)=1-p_{\bbeta}(y_i\mid\bx_i)σ(−mi​)=1−pβ​(yi​∣xi​) is the probability the model currently gives to the wrong label.

  • Badly misclassified (mi=−3m_i=-3mi​=−3): weight 0.950.950.95, a full-strength push.
  • On the boundary (mi=0m_i=0mi​=0): weight 0.50.50.5.
  • Confidently correct (mi=3m_i=3mi​=3): weight 0.050.050.05, almost ignored.

Compare with least squares (Course II), where the weight is the residual itself and grows without bound. Here every example's pull is capped at ∥xi∥\norm{\bx_i}∥xi​∥, and well-classified examples stop pulling: the logistic loss focuses on the hard cases.

Hence

∇F(β)=1nX⊤(π−y~)=1n∑i(πi−y~i⏟prediction error) xi.\displaystyle \nabla F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\bX\T(\bpi-\tilde\by)=\frac1n\sum_i\big(\underbrace{\pi_i-\tilde y_i}_{\text{prediction error}}\big)\,\bx_i.∇F(β)=n1​X⊤(π−y~​)=n1​i∑​(prediction errorπi​−y~​i​​​)xi​.

Same shape as least squares, 1nX⊤(Xβ−y)\frac1n\bX\T(\bX\bbeta-\by)n1​X⊤(Xβ−y): "prediction minus target, times the input". At the optimum the prediction errors are uncorrelated with every feature; in particular (thanks to the intercept) the predicted probabilities sum to the number of positive labels.

Curvature and the Lipschitz constant LLL

The slide states that ∇F\nabla F∇F is Lipschitz continuous with L=14n∥X∥22L=\frac1{4n}\norm{\bX}_2^2L=4n1​∥X∥22​, where ∥X∥2\norm{\bX}_2∥X∥2​ is the largest singular value of X\bXX (so ∥X∥22=λmax⁡(X⊤X)\norm{\bX}_2^2=\lambda_{\max}(\bX\T\bX)∥X∥22​=λmax​(X⊤X)). Here is where it comes from.

Derivation · Hessian and LLL

  1. Differentiate ∇ℓi(β)=−yixiσ(−mi)\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)=-y_i\bx_i\sigma(-m_i)∇ℓi​(β)=−yi​xi​σ(−mi​) once more: ∇2ℓi(β)=−yixi σ′(−mi) (−yixi⊤)=σ(mi)σ(−mi) xixi⊤\nabla^2\ell_i(\bbeta)=-y_i\bx_i\,\sigma'(-m_i)\,(-y_i\bx_i\T)=\sigma(m_i)\sigma(-m_i)\,\bx_i\bx_i\T∇2ℓi​(β)=−yi​xi​σ′(−mi​)(−yi​xi⊤​)=σ(mi​)σ(−mi​)xi​xi⊤​, using yi2=1y_i^2=1yi2​=1 and σ′(u)=σ(u)σ(−u)\sigma'(u)=\sigma(u)\sigma(-u)σ′(u)=σ(u)σ(−u).
  2. Averaging: ∇2F(β)=1nX⊤DX\nabla^2F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\bX\T\bD\bX∇2F(β)=n1​X⊤DX with D=Diag⁡(σ(mi)σ(−mi))\bD=\Diag\big(\sigma(m_i)\sigma(-m_i)\big)D=Diag(σ(mi​)σ(−mi​)). All diagonal entries are positive, so ∇2F⪰0\nabla^2F\succeq0∇2F⪰0: FFF is convex.
  3. Each entry of D\bDD is at most 14\tfrac1441​, so v⊤∇2F v=1n∑iDii(xi⊤v)2≤14n∥Xv∥2≤λmax⁡(X⊤X)4n∥v∥2\bv\T\nabla^2F\,\bv=\frac1n\sum_iD_{ii}(\bx_i\T\bv)^2\le\frac1{4n}\norm{\bX\bv}^2\le\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\bX\T\bX)}{4n}\norm{\bv}^2v⊤∇2Fv=n1​∑i​Dii​(xi⊤​v)2≤4n1​∥Xv∥2≤4nλmax​(X⊤X)​∥v∥2.

The factor 14\tfrac1441​ is the maximum slope of the sigmoid (figure in §3). Compared with the least-squares objective 12n∥Xβ−y∥2\frac1{2n}\norm{\bX\bbeta-\by}^22n1​∥Xβ−y∥2, whose Hessian is exactly 1nX⊤X\frac1n\bX\T\bXn1​X⊤X, the logistic objective is at most a quarter as curved, and much flatter where the margins are large.

Gradient descent

There is no closed form: setting ∇F=0\nabla F=\bzero∇F=0 gives d+1d+1d+1 nonlinear equations ∑i(πi−y~i)xi=0\sum_i(\pi_i-\tilde y_i)\bx_i=\bzero∑i​(πi​−y~​i​)xi​=0 (compare with the linear normal equations of Course II). Instead, iterate:

Slide p. 14 · with 0<γ<2/L0<\gamma<2/L0<γ<2/L

β(t+1)=β(t)−γ ∇F(β(t)).\displaystyle \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma\,\nabla F\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big).β(t+1)=β(t)−γ∇F(β(t)).

Why 0<γ<2/L0<\gamma<2/L0<γ<2/L works Beyond the slides

The descent lemma (§0) with β′=β−γ∇F(β)\bbeta'=\bbeta-\gamma\nabla F(\bbeta)β′=β−γ∇F(β) gives

F(β−γ∇F(β))≤F(β)−γ∥∇F(β)∥2+Lγ22∥∇F(β)∥2=F(β)−γ(1−Lγ2)∥∇F(β)∥2.\displaystyle F\big(\bbeta-\gamma\nabla F(\bbeta)\big)\le F(\bbeta)-\gamma\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta)}^2+\frac{L\gamma^2}2\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta)}^2=F(\bbeta)-\gamma\Big(1-\frac{L\gamma}2\Big)\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta)}^2.F(β−γ∇F(β))≤F(β)−γ∥∇F(β)∥2+2Lγ2​∥∇F(β)∥2=F(β)−γ(1−2Lγ​)∥∇F(β)∥2.

For 0<γ<2/L0<\gamma<2/L0<γ<2/L the bracket is positive, so FFF decreases at every step by an amount proportional to ∥∇F∥2\norm{\nabla F}^2∥∇F∥2. Summing over steps, ∑t∥∇F(β(t))∥2<∞\sum_t\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})}^2<\infty∑t​​∇F(β(t))​2<∞, so the gradient tends to zero; by convexity, the iterates approach the minimizers (when a minimizer exists, see below). With γ=1/L\gamma=1/Lγ=1/L the decrease per step is at least 12L∥∇F∥2\frac1{2L}\norm{\nabla F}^22L1​∥∇F∥2, and F(β(t))−F⋆≤L∥β(0)−β⋆∥22tF(\bbeta^{(t)})-F^\star\le\frac{L\norm{\bbeta^{(0)}-\bbeta^\star}^2}{2t}F(β(t))−F⋆≤2tL∥β(0)−β⋆∥2​.

Newton's method is IRLS Beyond the slides

Gradient descent only uses first derivatives. Newton's method uses the Hessian: β←β−(∇2F)−1∇F=β+(X⊤DX)−1X⊤(y~−π)\bbeta\leftarrow\bbeta-(\nabla^2F)^{-1}\nabla F=\bbeta+(\bX\T\bD\bX)^{-1}\bX\T(\tilde\by-\bpi)β←β−(∇2F)−1∇F=β+(X⊤DX)−1X⊤(y~​−π). Rearranging,

βnew=(X⊤DX)−1X⊤D z,z=Xβ+D−1(y~−π),D=Diag⁡(πi(1−πi)),\displaystyle {\bbeta_{\text{new}}=(\bX\T\bD\bX)^{-1}\bX\T\bD\,\bz,}\qquad\allowbreak { \bz=\bX\bbeta+\bD^{-1}(\tilde\by-\bpi),}\qquad\allowbreak { \bD=\Diag\big(\pi_i(1-\pi_i)\big),}βnew​=(X⊤DX)−1X⊤Dz,z=Xβ+D−1(y~​−π),D=Diag(πi​(1−πi​)),

(check: X⊤Dz=X⊤DXβ+X⊤(y~−π)\bX\T\bD\bz=\bX\T\bD\bX\bbeta+\bX\T(\tilde\by-\bpi)X⊤Dz=X⊤DXβ+X⊤(y~​−π)). Each Newton step is a weighted least-squares problem with weights πi(1−πi)\pi_i(1-\pi_i)πi​(1−πi​) and a "working response" z\bzz: exactly the IRLS template of Course II, §8, here derived from Newton's method instead of majorization. On example A it converges in about four iterations (0.8→1.110→1.2061→1.21398→1.214030.8\to1.110\to1.2061\to1.21398\to1.214030.8→1.110→1.2061→1.21398→1.21403). Gradient descent needs 28 iterations to match the fourth of these, and after 12 it is only as close as Newton's third. Each iteration costs O(nd2+d3)O(nd^2+d^3)O(nd2+d3), though, which is why large-scale problems use the first-order methods of Part 2.

When the minimizer does not exist Beyond the slides

Suppose the data are linearly separable: some βˉ\bar\bbetaβˉ​ gives every example a positive margin. Then for c>0c>0c>0, F(cβˉ)=1n∑ilog⁡(1+e−cmˉi)→0F(c\bar\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_i\log(1+e^{-c\bar m_i})\to0F(cβˉ​)=n1​∑i​log(1+e−cmˉi​)→0 as c→∞c\to\inftyc→∞, yet F>0F>0F>0 for every finite β\bbetaβ. The infimum is not attained: there is no maximum-likelihood estimate. Gradient descent keeps decreasing FFF by inflating ∥β∥\norm{\bbeta}∥β∥ (the norm grows like log⁡t\log tlogt, while the direction slowly approaches the maximum-margin separator), and the predicted probabilities become overconfident 0s and 1s.

The standard fix is regularization, exactly as in Course II: minimize F(β)+λ2∥β1:d∥2F(\bbeta)+\frac\lambda2\norm{\bbeta_{1:d}}^2F(β)+2λ​∥β1:d​∥2. The penalty makes the objective strongly convex in the weights, guarantees a unique minimizer, keeps the predicted probabilities away from 0 and 1, and adds λ\lambdaλ to the constant LLL. Penalizing with λ∥β1:d∥1\lambda\norm{\bbeta_{1:d}}_1λ∥β1:d​∥1​ instead gives sparse logistic regression, solved by proximal gradient with soft thresholding (Course II, §6).

Logistic regression by gradient descent
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(u):
    return 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(0.5 * u))          # same as 1/(1+exp(-u)), never overflows

def logistic_loss_grad(beta, X, y):
    """X: (n, d+1) design matrix with a column of ones, y in {-1, +1}."""
    m = y * (X @ beta)                            # margins m_i
    F = np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, -m))              # mean of log(1 + exp(-m_i)), stable
    g = -(X.T @ (y * sigmoid(-m))) / len(y)       # (1/n) sum of -y_i x_i sigma(-m_i)
    return F, g

def gd_logistic(X, y, n_iter=200):
    L = np.linalg.norm(X, 2) ** 2 / (4 * len(y))  # Lipschitz constant ||X||^2 / (4n)
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        beta -= (1 / L) * logistic_loss_grad(beta, X, y)[1]
    return beta

h = np.arange(1, 7.); X = np.column_stack([np.ones(6), h - 3.5]); y = np.array([-1, -1, 1, -1, 1, 1.])
print(gd_logistic(X, y))                          # [0.     1.2140...]  (worked example A)

With m=yixi⊤βm=y_i\bx_i\T\bbetam=yi​xi⊤​β: ddmlog⁡(1+e−m)=−e−m1+e−m=−σ(−m)\frac{\dd}{\dd m}\log(1+e^{-m})=\frac{-e^{-m}}{1+e^{-m}}=-\sigma(-m)dmd​log(1+e−m)=1+e−m−e−m​=−σ(−m) and ∇βm=yixi\nabla_{\bbeta}m=y_i\bx_i∇β​m=yi​xi​, so ∇ℓi=−yixiσ(−yixi⊤β)\nabla\ell_i=-y_i\bx_i\sigma(-y_i\bx_i\T\bbeta)∇ℓi​=−yi​xi​σ(−yi​xi⊤​β).

The Hessian is 1nX⊤Diag⁡(σ(mi)σ(−mi))X\frac1n\bX\T\Diag(\sigma(m_i)\sigma(-m_i))\bXn1​X⊤Diag(σ(mi​)σ(−mi​))X and σ(m)σ(−m)=σ(m)(1−σ(m))≤14\sigma(m)\sigma(-m)=\sigma(m)(1-\sigma(m))\le\tfrac14σ(m)σ(−m)=σ(m)(1−σ(m))≤41​ (maximum of p(1−p)p(1-p)p(1−p) at p=12p=\tfrac12p=21​), so ∇2F⪯14nX⊤X⪯∥X∥224nI\nabla^2F\preceq\frac1{4n}\bX\T\bX\preceq\frac{\norm{\bX}_2^2}{4n}\bI∇2F⪯4n1​X⊤X⪯4n∥X∥22​​I.

4.3Why does every logistic regression have ∇F(0)=−12n∑iyixi\nabla F(\bzero)=-\frac1{2n}\sum_iy_i\bx_i∇F(0)=−2n1​∑i​yi​xi​?

At β=0\bbeta=\bzeroβ=0 every margin is 0 and σ(0)=12\sigma(0)=\tfrac12σ(0)=21​, so each term is −12yixi-\tfrac12y_i\bx_i−21​yi​xi​. The first step of gradient descent from zero moves β\bbetaβ toward the label-weighted average of the inputs.

4.4The training data are linearly separable. What does gradient descent do, and how do you fix it?

No minimizer exists (F→0F\to0F→0 only as ∥β∥→∞\norm{\bbeta}\to\infty∥β∥→∞), so the iterates grow without bound while their direction converges to the maximum-margin separator, and the probabilities saturate at 0 and 1. Adding a ridge penalty λ2∥β1:d∥2\frac\lambda2\norm{\bbeta_{1:d}}^22λ​∥β1:d​∥2 restores a unique, finite minimizer.

4.5Explain in words the factor σ(−mi)\sigma(-m_i)σ(−mi​) in the gradient.

It is the probability the model assigns to the wrong label of example iii. Misclassified examples (close to 1) push β\bbetaβ hard; confidently correct ones (close to 0) barely contribute.

§5Slides pp. 15–21

Multiclass classification: softmax and cross-entropy

With KKK classes, give each class its own linear score, turn the KKK scores into probabilities with the softmax, and minimize the negative log-probability of the true class. Binary logistic regression is the case K=2K=2K=2.

From Bernoulli to categorical

Binary logistic regression uses a Bernoulli distribution. For K>2K>2K>2 classes we use its multiclass analogue, the categorical distribution. The label Yi∈{1,…,K}Y_i\in\{1,\dots,K\}Yi​∈{1,…,K} is represented by its one-hot encoding:

Slide p. 15

yi∈{0,1}K,yi,k=1{Yi=k},∑k=1Kyi,k=1.\displaystyle {\by_i\in\{0,1\}^K,}\qquad\allowbreak { y_{i,k}=\ind_{\{Y_i=k\}},}\qquad\allowbreak { \sum_{k=1}^Ky_{i,k}=1.}yi​∈{0,1}K,yi,k​=1{Yi​=k}​,k=1∑K​yi,k​=1.

For example, with K=3K=3K=3 the label "class 2" is yi=(0,1,0)\by_i=(0,1,0)yi​=(0,1,0). The vector has exactly one 1, in the position of the true class.

One score per class

Each class gets its own coefficient vector, collected as the columns of a matrix (slide p. 16):

βk∈Rd+1,k=1,…,K,B=[β1,…,βK]∈R(d+1)×K,ui,k=xi⊤βk.\displaystyle {\bbeta_k\in\R^{d+1},}\quad\allowbreak { k=1,\dots,K,}\qquad\allowbreak { \bB=[\bbeta_1,\dots,\bbeta_K]\in\R^{(d+1)\times K},}\qquad\allowbreak { u_{i,k}=\bx_i\T\bbeta_k.}βk​∈Rd+1,k=1,…,K,B=[β1​,…,βK​]∈R(d+1)×K,ui,k​=xi⊤​βk​.

The row vector of scores of example iii is xi⊤B=(ui,1,…,ui,K)\bx_i\T\bB=(u_{i,1},\dots,u_{i,K})xi⊤​B=(ui,1​,…,ui,K​); for the whole dataset, U=XB∈Rn×K\bU=\bX\bB\in\R^{n\times K}U=XB∈Rn×K. A higher score means "more like class kkk".

The softmax

The softmax turns the KKK scores into probabilities:

Slide p. 17

pi,k=P(Y=k∣X=xi)=exp⁡(ui,k)∑ℓ=1Kexp⁡(ui,ℓ),Yi∣Xi=xi ∼ Categorical⁡(pi,1,…,pi,K).\displaystyle p_{i,k}=P(Y=k\mid X=\bx_i)=\frac{\exp(u_{i,k})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(u_{i,\ell})},\qquad\allowbreak {Y_i\mid X_i=\bx_i}\ \sim\ \allowbreak\Cat(p_{i,1},\dots,p_{i,K}).pi,k​=P(Y=k∣X=xi​)=∑ℓ=1K​exp(ui,ℓ​)exp(ui,k​)​,Yi​∣Xi​=xi​ ∼ Categorical(pi,1​,…,pi,K​).

Exponentiate (everything becomes positive), then normalize (everything sums to 1): hence pi,k≥0p_{i,k}\ge0pi,k​≥0 and ∑kpi,k=1\sum_kp_{i,k}=1∑k​pi,k​=1. The name says what it does: it is a smooth version of "put all the probability on the largest score".

Derivation · properties of the softmax

  1. Order-preserving. exp⁡\expexp is increasing, so the largest score gets the largest probability. Hence the predicted class (slide p. 18):
    y^i=argmax⁡k pi,k=argmax⁡k ui,k.\displaystyle \widehat y_i=\argmax_k\,p_{i,k}=\argmax_k\,u_{i,k}.y​i​=kargmax​pi,k​=kargmax​ui,k​.
  2. Shift-invariant. Adding the same constant ccc to every score multiplies numerator and denominator by ece^cec: euk+c∑ℓeuℓ+c=euk∑ℓeuℓ\frac{e^{u_k+c}}{\sum_\ell e^{u_\ell+c}}=\frac{e^{u_k}}{\sum_\ell e^{u_\ell}}∑ℓ​euℓ​+ceuk​+c​=∑ℓ​euℓ​euk​​. Only differences of scores matter. Consequently, adding the same vector to every βk\bbeta_kβk​ changes nothing: the parameters are not identifiable, and one can fix βK=0\bbeta_K=\bzeroβK​=0 without loss of generality (or add a ridge penalty, which picks one representative).
  3. K=2K=2K=2 is logistic regression. pi,1=eu1eu1+eu2=11+e−(u1−u2)=σ(xi⊤(β1−β2))p_{i,1}=\frac{e^{u_1}}{e^{u_1}+e^{u_2}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(u_1-u_2)}}=\sigma\big(\bx_i\T(\bbeta_1-\bbeta_2)\big)pi,1​=eu1​+eu2​eu1​​=1+e−(u1​−u2​)1​=σ(xi⊤​(β1​−β2​)): the sigmoid of the difference of the two scores. Binary logistic regression with β=β1−β2\bbeta=\bbeta_1-\bbeta_2β=β1​−β2​.
  4. Scale = confidence. Multiplying all scores by c>1c>1c>1 makes the softmax sharper (closer to one-hot), c<1c<1c<1 makes it flatter (closer to uniform). As for binary scores, the length of the coefficients controls confidence.
∎

Decision regions

Class kkk wins where uk(x)≥uℓ(x)u_k(\bx)\ge u_\ell(\bx)uk​(x)≥uℓ​(x) for every ℓ\ellℓ, i.e. where x⊤(βk−βℓ)≥0\bx\T(\bbeta_k-\bbeta_\ell)\ge0x⊤(βk​−βℓ​)≥0 for all ℓ≠k\ell\neq kℓ=k: an intersection of half-spaces, hence a convex polyhedral region. The boundary between classes kkk and ℓ\ellℓ is the hyperplane x⊤(βk−βℓ)=0\bx\T(\bbeta_k-\bbeta_\ell)=0x⊤(βk​−βℓ​)=0, the binary boundary of §1 for the pair.

The cross-entropy loss

For a one-hot label, the categorical probability of the observed class is ∏kpi,kyi,k\prod_kp_{i,k}^{y_{i,k}}∏k​pi,kyi,k​​, and its negative logarithm is

Slide p. 18

ℓi(B)=−∑k=1Kyi,klog⁡pi,k.\displaystyle \ell_i(\bB)=-\sum_{k=1}^Ky_{i,k}\log p_{i,k}.ℓi​(B)=−k=1∑K​yi,k​logpi,k​.

All but one yi,ky_{i,k}yi,k​ vanish, so only the probability assigned to the true class contributes to the loss: if cic_ici​ is the true class, ℓi(B)=−log⁡pi,ci\ell_i(\bB)=-\log p_{i,c_i}ℓi​(B)=−logpi,ci​​. This is the cross-entropy loss (slide p. 19), the negative log-likelihood of the categorical model. The empirical objective is the average:

Slide p. 20

F(B)=1n∑i=1nℓi(B).\displaystyle F(\bB)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\bB).F(B)=n1​i=1∑n​ℓi​(B).

It is smooth and convex in B\bBB.

Binary logistic regression ⟶ multinomial logistic regression.

The log-sum-exp form Beyond the slides

Substituting the softmax into −log⁡pi,ci-\log p_{i,c_i}−logpi,ci​​:

ℓi(B)=−ui,ci+LSE⁡(ui),LSE⁡(u)=log⁡∑k=1Keuk.\displaystyle {\ell_i(\bB)=-u_{i,c_i}+\LSE(\bu_i),}\qquad\allowbreak { \LSE(\bu)=\log\sum_{k=1}^Ke^{u_k}.}ℓi​(B)=−ui,ci​​+LSE(ui​),LSE(u)=logk=1∑K​euk​.

The log-sum-exp is a smooth maximum: max⁡kuk≤LSE⁡(u)≤max⁡kuk+log⁡K\max_ku_k\le\LSE(\bu)\le\max_ku_k+\log Kmaxk​uk​≤LSE(u)≤maxk​uk​+logK. With ccc the true class, max⁡kuk−uc≤ℓ≤max⁡kuk−uc+log⁡K\max_ku_k-u_c\le\ell\le\max_ku_k-u_c+\log Kmaxk​uk​−uc​≤ℓ≤maxk​uk​−uc​+logK, where max⁡kuk−uc=max⁡(0, best competing score−uc)\max_ku_k-u_c=\max\big(0,\ \text{best competing score}-u_c\big)maxk​uk​−uc​=max(0, best competing score−uc​). So the cross-entropy is a smoothed measure of how far the true class lags behind its best competitor (zero once it is ahead), just as the logistic loss is a smoothed max⁡(0,−m)\max(0,-m)max(0,−m). It is small when the true class beats all others by a wide gap. Two practical consequences:

  • Numerical stability. euke^{u_k}euk​ overflows for scores of a few hundred. By shift invariance, compute LSE⁡(u)=max⁡kuk+log⁡∑keuk−max⁡ℓuℓ\LSE(\bu)=\max_ku_k+\log\sum_ke^{u_k-\max_\ell u_\ell}LSE(u)=maxk​uk​+log∑k​euk​−maxℓ​uℓ​: every exponent is now ≤0\le0≤0.
  • Never compute log⁡\loglog of a softmax output. Compute the log-probabilities as ui,k−LSE⁡(ui)u_{i,k}-\LSE(\bu_i)ui,k​−LSE(ui​) directly; a probability that underflows to 0 would give log⁡0=−∞\log0=-\inftylog0=−∞.

The Hessian of LSE⁡\LSELSE is Diag⁡(p)−pp⊤\Diag(\bp)-\bp\bp\TDiag(p)−pp⊤, and for any v\bvv, v⊤(Diag⁡(p)−pp⊤)v=∑kpkvk2−(∑kpkvk)2\bv\T(\Diag(\bp)-\bp\bp\T)\bv=\sum_kp_kv_k^2-\big(\sum_kp_kv_k\big)^2v⊤(Diag(p)−pp⊤)v=∑k​pk​vk2​−(∑k​pk​vk​)2, the variance of vvv under the distribution p\bpp, hence ≥0\ge0≥0. ∎

Once again: prediction minus target, times the input. Least squares, binary logistic regression and multinomial logistic regression all have gradients of the form 1nX⊤(predictions−targets)\frac1n\bX\T(\text{predictions}-\text{targets})n1​X⊤(predictions−targets). The gradient step raises the score of the true class (where p−y<0p-y<0p−y<0) and lowers the others in proportion to the probability they wrongly received.

Softmax regression: stable cross-entropy and its gradient
import numpy as np

def log_softmax(U):
    U = U - U.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)          # shift invariance: avoids overflow
    return U - np.log(np.exp(U).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))

def cross_entropy_grad(B, X, Y):
    """X: (n, d+1), Y: (n, K) one-hot labels, B: (d+1, K) coefficients."""
    logP = log_softmax(X @ B)
    F = -np.mean(np.sum(Y * logP, axis=1))        # only the true class contributes
    G = X.T @ (np.exp(logP) - Y) / len(X)         # (1/n) X^T (P - Y)
    return F, G

B = np.array([[0., 1., 0.5], [1., 0., -0.5]])     # columns beta_1, beta_2, beta_3
print(cross_entropy_grad(B, np.array([[1., 2.]]), np.array([[0, 1., 0]])))   # loss 1.3715 (example B)

§6Slides pp. 22–25

From full gradient to stochastic optimization

When the objective is an average over millions of examples, an exact gradient is an expensive luxury. A gradient computed on a few random examples is cheap, roughly right, and wrong in a random way.

The finite-sum structure

Many machine-learning problems share the finite-sum structure

For logistic regression, ℓi\ell_iℓi​ is the loss associated with observation (xi,yi)(\bx_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​), and its gradient costs O(d)O(d)O(d): one inner product and one scaled copy of xi\bx_ixi​.

The cost of a full gradient

Gradient descent uses ∇F(β)=1n∑i=1n∇ℓi(β)\nabla F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)∇F(β)=n1​∑i=1n​∇ℓi​(β), so every iteration processes all nnn observations: O(nd)O(nd)O(nd) work per step. With n=107n=10^7n=107 examples and d=103d=10^3d=103 features that is 101010^{10}1010 operations for a single step, and gradient descent needs hundreds of steps. When nnn is very large:

Slide p. 24

accurate gradient⟺expensive iteration.\displaystyle {\text{accurate gradient}}\quad\allowbreak {\Longleftrightarrow}\quad\allowbreak {\text{expensive iteration.}}accurate gradient⟺expensive iteration.

Key idea (slide p. 25): can we make progress using only a small random subset of the data at each iteration? We would get

cheaper but noisy gradient estimates.\displaystyle \text{cheaper but noisy gradient estimates.}cheaper but noisy gradient estimates.

Intuition · why a few examples are enough to start

  • Redundancy. Imagine your dataset is ten copies of the same 100 000 examples. Gradient descent pays ten times more per step for exactly the same direction. A method that looks at one random example per step is not affected at all. Real datasets are not literal copies, but they are highly redundant: many examples "say the same thing".
  • Far from the optimum, everyone agrees. When β\bbetaβ is bad, most individual gradients point in roughly the same direction as the full gradient, so a single example already gives a useful direction. Near the optimum the individual gradients disagree and cancel out; that is where the noise will hurt (§8).
  • We do not need 10 digits. The training loss is itself a noisy estimate of the error on new data, with a statistical error of order 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​ or so. Optimizing far below that precision buys nothing.

To compare methods fairly we count epochs: one epoch is nnn evaluations of individual gradients ∇ℓi\nabla\ell_i∇ℓi​, the cost of a single full gradient. One step of gradient descent costs one epoch; one step of SGD costs 1/n1/n1/n of an epoch.

§7Slides pp. 26–28

Stochastic gradient descent

Pick one example at random, take a step along its gradient. On average that step points exactly where gradient descent would go.

The algorithm

Consider F(β)=1n∑i=1nℓi(β)F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\bbeta)F(β)=n1​∑i=1n​ℓi​(β). At iteration ttt, sample an index it∼U{1,…,n}i_t\sim\cU\{1,\dots,n\}it​∼U{1,…,n} (uniformly at random), and use the gradient of that single observation:

Slide p. 26 · stochastic gradient descent (SGD)

β(t+1)=β(t)−γt ∇ℓit(β(t)).\displaystyle \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma_t\,\nabla\ell_{i_t}\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big).β(t+1)=β(t)−γt​∇ℓit​​(β(t)).

Each step costs O(d)O(d)O(d), independently of nnn. The step size γt\gamma_tγt​ (the learning rate) may change with ttt; §10 explains why it usually should.

Why it is a reasonable approximation of gradient descent

Conditionally on the current iterate, the only randomness is the index iti_tit​, which takes each value iii with probability 1n\frac1nn1​:

Slide p. 27

Eit[∇ℓit(β(t))]=∑i=1n1n ∇ℓi(β(t))=∇F(β(t)).\displaystyle \E_{i_t}\Big[\nabla\ell_{i_t}\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big)\Big]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1n\,\nabla\ell_i\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big)=\nabla F\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big).Eit​​[∇ℓit​​(β(t))]=i=1∑n​n1​∇ℓi​(β(t))=∇F(β(t)).

The stochastic gradient is therefore an unbiased but noisy estimate of the full gradient (slide p. 28).

  • Unbiased: on average, SGD moves in the gradient-descent direction. No systematic drift.
  • Noisy: any single step can point quite far from −∇F-\nabla F−∇F, even uphill. §8 quantifies the noise.
  • The unbiasedness relies on uniform sampling and on FFF being the average of the ℓi\ell_iℓi​. With non-uniform probabilities qiq_iqi​, the estimate ∇ℓi/(nqi)\nabla\ell_i/(nq_i)∇ℓi​/(nqi​) is unbiased again (importance sampling).

SGD for logistic regression

With ∇ℓi(β)=−σ(−mi) yixi\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)=-\sigma(-m_i)\,y_i\bx_i∇ℓi​(β)=−σ(−mi​)yi​xi​, the SGD step reads

β(t+1)=β(t)+γt σ(−mit) yitxit.\displaystyle \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}+\gamma_t\,\sigma(-m_{i_t})\,y_{i_t}\bx_{i_t}.β(t+1)=β(t)+γt​σ(−mit​​)yit​​xit​​.

Look at one example, push the boundary so as to increase its margin, harder if it is misclassified. The classical perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958) does the same with weight 1 for misclassified examples and 0 otherwise: it is SGD on the loss max⁡(0,−m)\max(0,-m)max(0,−m) with step 1.

SGD is not a descent method Beyond the slides

A single SGD step can increase FFF. What decreases is the expected value, when the step is small enough:

Derivation · expected one-step progress

Write gt=∇ℓit(β(t))\bg_t=\nabla\ell_{i_t}(\bbeta^{(t)})gt​=∇ℓit​​(β(t)). The descent lemma with β′=β(t)−γtgt\bbeta'=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma_t\bg_tβ′=β(t)−γt​gt​ gives F(β(t+1))≤F(β(t))−γt∇F(β(t))⊤gt+Lγt22∥gt∥2F(\bbeta^{(t+1)})\le F(\bbeta^{(t)})-\gamma_t\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})\T\bg_t+\frac{L\gamma_t^2}2\norm{\bg_t}^2F(β(t+1))≤F(β(t))−γt​∇F(β(t))⊤gt​+2Lγt2​​∥gt​∥2. Take the conditional expectation and use E[gt∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t))\E[\bg_t\mid\bbeta^{(t)}]=\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})E[gt​∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t)):

E[F(β(t+1)) ∣ β(t)]≤F(β(t))−γt∥∇F(β(t))∥2⏟progress+Lγt22 E[∥gt∥2 ∣ β(t)]⏟price of the noise.\displaystyle \E\big[F(\bbeta^{(t+1)})\,\big|\,\bbeta^{(t)}\big]\le F(\bbeta^{(t)})-\underbrace{\gamma_t\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})}^2}_{\text{progress}}+\allowbreak\underbrace{\frac{L\gamma_t^2}2\,\E\big[\norm{\bg_t}^2\,\big|\,\bbeta^{(t)}\big]}_{\text{price of the noise}}.E[F(β(t+1))​β(t)]≤F(β(t))−progressγt​​∇F(β(t))​2​​+price of the noise2Lγt2​​E[∥gt​∥2​β(t)]​​.
∎

Progress is first order in γt\gamma_tγt​, the noise penalty second order. Far from the optimum, ∥∇F∥2\norm{\nabla F}^2∥∇F∥2 is large and progress wins. Near the optimum, ∇F≈0\nabla F\approx\bzero∇F≈0 but E∥gt∥2\E\norm{\bg_t}^2E∥gt​∥2 does not vanish, and the noise term wins unless γt\gamma_tγt​ shrinks. That tension drives all of §8–§13.

Step 1 uses student 3 (passed after 3 hours). To raise its margin, SGD makes the slope negative, which is the wrong direction for the data as a whole: FFF rises from 0.6930.6930.693 to 0.7790.7790.779. Steps 2 and 3 repair this. Step 4 uses student 4 (failed after 4 hours) and pulls the slope back down: FFF rises again. Cheap, unbiased, noisy.

How to sample in practice Beyond the slides

  • With replacement (independent uniform indices): the version analysed in theory.
  • Random reshuffling: shuffle the data once per epoch and go through it in order. Every example is used exactly once per epoch; usually as good or better, and the default in deep-learning libraries.
  • Fixed cyclic order: risky. If the file is sorted by class, SGD sees thousands of positives, then thousands of negatives, and oscillates.

SGD also works on a stream of data: if each example is used only once, the stochastic gradients are unbiased for the gradient of the expected loss over the data distribution, so SGD then directly minimizes the population risk rather than the training loss.

7.3In worked example C, why did the full objective increase after the first step?

The step only looks at student 3, an atypical example (passed with little study). Increasing its margin requires lowering the slope, which hurts the four typical students. The single-example gradient was a poor (though unbiased) estimate of the full gradient.

§8Slides pp. 29–32

Stochastic gradient noise

The stochastic gradient is the true gradient plus a zero-mean error. Far from the solution the error is a nuisance; near the solution it dominates, and with a constant step SGD ends up wandering in a ball around the minimizer instead of converging to it.

Signal plus noise

Define the stochastic gradient used at step ttt:

Slides pp. 29–30

gt=∇ℓit(β(t)),E[gt∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t)),gt=∇F(β(t))+ξt,E[ξt∣β(t)]=0.\displaystyle {\bg_t=\nabla\ell_{i_t}\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big),}\qquad\allowbreak { \E\big[\bg_t\mid\bbeta^{(t)}\big]=\nabla F\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big),}\qquad\allowbreak { \bg_t=\nabla F\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big)+\bxi_t,}\quad\allowbreak { \E\big[\bxi_t\mid\bbeta^{(t)}\big]=\bzero.}gt​=∇ℓit​​(β(t)),E[gt​∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t)),gt​=∇F(β(t))+ξt​,E[ξt​∣β(t)]=0.

ξt\bxi_tξt​ is the gradient noise: the gap between what this particular example says and what the whole dataset says. Its variability can be measured by its conditional variance:

Slide p. 31

E[∥ξt∥2 ∣ β(t)].\displaystyle \E\Big[\norm{\bxi_t}^2\,\Big|\,\bbeta^{(t)}\Big].E[∥ξt​∥2​β(t)].

For uniform sampling it can be written out explicitly Beyond the slides:

E[∥ξt∥2 ∣ β(t)]=1n∑i=1n∥∇ℓi(β(t))−∇F(β(t))∥2=1n∑i=1n∥∇ℓi(β(t))∥2−∥∇F(β(t))∥2.\displaystyle \E\Big[\norm{\bxi_t}^2\,\Big|\,\bbeta^{(t)}\Big]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\norm{\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta^{(t)})-\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})}^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\norm{\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta^{(t)})}^2-\norm{\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})}^2.E[∥ξt​∥2​β(t)]=n1​i=1∑n​​∇ℓi​(β(t))−∇F(β(t))​2=n1​i=1∑n​​∇ℓi​(β(t))​2−​∇F(β(t))​2.

Derivation

Given β(t)\bbeta^{(t)}β(t), ξt\bxi_tξt​ takes the value ∇ℓi−∇F\nabla\ell_i-\nabla F∇ℓi​−∇F with probability 1n\frac1nn1​, which gives the first expression. Expanding the square, 1n∑i∥∇ℓi∥2−2∇F⊤(1n∑i∇ℓi)+∥∇F∥2=1n∑i∥∇ℓi∥2−∥∇F∥2\frac1n\sum_i\norm{\nabla\ell_i}^2-2\nabla F\T\big(\frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell_i\big)+\norm{\nabla F}^2=\frac1n\sum_i\norm{\nabla\ell_i}^2-\norm{\nabla F}^2n1​∑i​∥∇ℓi​∥2−2∇F⊤(n1​∑i​∇ℓi​)+∥∇F∥2=n1​∑i​∥∇ℓi​∥2−∥∇F∥2: "mean of squares minus square of the mean", as for any variance.

∎

Large gradient variance means that successive SGD directions may differ substantially: the path zig-zags. SGD trades computational cost per iteration for gradient noise.

The noise does not vanish at the solution

At a minimizer β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ the full gradient is zero, but the individual gradients are not: each example would like the boundary somewhere else, and their wishes only cancel on average. The noise level at the optimum is

σ⋆2=1n∑i=1n∥∇ℓi(β⋆)∥2,\displaystyle \sigma_\star^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\norm{\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta^\star)}^2,σ⋆2​=n1​i=1∑n​∥∇ℓi​(β⋆)∥2,

which is positive unless every single ℓi\ell_iℓi​ is minimized at β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ (the "interpolation" regime, e.g. a model that fits every training example perfectly). In worked example A, at β^=(0,1.214)\widehat\bbeta=(0,1.214)β​=(0,1.214), the six individual gradients are −σ(−mi)yi(1,xi)-\sigma(-m_i)y_i(1,x_i)−σ(−mi​)yi​(1,xi​) with weights (0.046,0.139,0.647,0.647,0.139,0.046)(0.046,0.139,0.647,0.647,0.139,0.046)(0.046,0.139,0.647,0.647,0.139,0.046): nowhere near zero, even though they sum to zero.

∎

Two terms, two regimes. The first forgets the starting point geometrically fast, like gradient descent: far from the solution, SGD makes quick progress. The second is a floor proportional to γ\gammaγ: near the solution, the iterates keep bouncing in a "noise ball" whose mean squared radius is of order γG2/μ\gamma G^2/\muγG2/μ. A smaller step shrinks the ball but slows the first phase. Escaping this dilemma is the job of decreasing step sizes (§10), averaging (§10) and variance reduction (§13).

8.2Why does constant-step SGD not converge to β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆, while gradient descent does?

At β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ the full gradient vanishes, so gradient descent stops there. The stochastic gradient does not vanish (noise level σ⋆2>0\sigma_\star^2>0σ⋆2​>0), so SGD keeps taking steps of size about γσ⋆\gamma\sigma_\starγσ⋆​ in random directions: it hovers in a ball of squared radius of order γ\gammaγ.

§9Slides pp. 33–36

Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent

Average the gradients of a small random batch instead of using a single one: the estimate stays unbiased, its variance drops in proportion to the batch size, and the cost per step rises in the same proportion.

Definition

Instead of one observation, sample a mini-batch Bt⊂{1,…,n}\cB_t\subset\{1,\dots,n\}Bt​⊂{1,…,n} of size ∣Bt∣=b\abs{\cB_t}=b∣Bt​∣=b and average its gradients:

Slide p. 33

gt=1b∑i∈Bt∇ℓi(β(t)),β(t+1)=β(t)−γt gt.\displaystyle {\bg_t=\frac1b\sum_{i\in\cB_t}\nabla\ell_i\big(\bbeta^{(t)}\big),}\qquad\allowbreak { \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma_t\,\bg_t.}gt​=b1​i∈Bt​∑​∇ℓi​(β(t)),β(t+1)=β(t)−γt​gt​.

With uniform sampling the estimate remains unbiased, E[gt∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t))\E[\bg_t\mid\bbeta^{(t)}]=\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})E[gt​∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t)) (slide p. 34).

Derivation

With replacement: gt\bg_tgt​ is the average of bbb independent single-example estimates, each unbiased, so it is unbiased. Without replacement (a uniformly random subset of size bbb): each index belongs to Bt\cB_tBt​ with probability b/nb/nb/n, so E[gt]=1b∑i=1nbn∇ℓi=1n∑i∇ℓi=∇F\E[\bg_t]=\frac1b\sum_{i=1}^n\frac bn\nabla\ell_i=\frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell_i=\nabla FE[gt​]=b1​∑i=1n​nb​∇ℓi​=n1​∑i​∇ℓi​=∇F.

∎

The trade-off

Slide p. 35 · increasing the batch size bbb gives

less gradient noise⟺more computation per iteration.\displaystyle {\text{less gradient noise}}\quad\allowbreak {\Longleftrightarrow}\quad\allowbreak {\text{more computation per iteration.}}less gradient noise⟺more computation per iteration.

Two extreme cases (slide p. 36): b=1b=1b=1 is standard SGD, b=nb=nb=n is full gradient descent. Quantitatively Beyond the slides, if σ2(β)=E∥∇ℓi(β)−∇F(β)∥2\sigma^2(\bbeta)=\E\norm{\nabla\ell_{i}(\bbeta)-\nabla F(\bbeta)}^2σ2(β)=E∥∇ℓi​(β)−∇F(β)∥2 denotes the single-example noise variance,

E[∥ξt∥2∣β(t)]=σ2(β(t))b  (with replacement),n−bn−1⋅σ2(β(t))b  (without replacement).\displaystyle \E\big[\norm{\bxi_t}^2\mid\bbeta^{(t)}\big]=\frac{\sigma^2(\bbeta^{(t)})}{b}\ \ \text{(with replacement)},\qquad\allowbreak \frac{n-b}{n-1}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2(\bbeta^{(t)})}{b}\ \ \text{(without replacement)}.E[∥ξt​∥2∣β(t)]=bσ2(β(t))​  (with replacement),n−1n−b​⋅bσ2(β(t))​  (without replacement).

The variance of an average of bbb independent draws is divided by bbb. Without replacement it is even smaller (the finite-population correction n−bn−1\frac{n-b}{n-1}n−1n−b​), and it reaches exactly zero at b=nb=nb=n, where the "estimate" is the full gradient. In the noise-ball bound of §8, the floor is γG2/(2μ)\gamma G^2/(2\mu)γG2/(2μ) with G2G^2G2 a bound on E∥gt∥2=∥∇F∥2+E∥ξt∥2\E\norm{\bg_t}^2=\norm{\nabla F}^2+\E\norm{\bxi_t}^2E∥gt​∥2=∥∇F∥2+E∥ξt​∥2. Near the solution ∇F≈0\nabla F\approx\bzero∇F≈0, so G2G^2G2 is essentially the noise variance: a batch of size bbb lowers the floor from about γσ2/(2μ)\gamma\sigma^2/(2\mu)γσ2/(2μ) to about γσ2/(2μb)\gamma\sigma^2/(2\mu b)γσ2/(2μb).

Intuition · is a bigger batch worth it?

  • Per unit of computation, often not. The standard deviation of the noise only falls like 1/b1/\sqrt b1/b​ while the cost grows like bbb. In the noise-dominated phase, one step with batch bbb and step bγb\gammabγ moves about as far, with about as much noise, as bbb plain SGD steps with step γ\gammaγ (the "linear scaling rule" of deep learning, valid up to a problem-dependent critical batch size).
  • Per unit of time, often yes. GPUs and vectorized code process 32, 256 or 1024 examples almost as fast as one. Up to that hardware limit, a larger batch is nearly free and gives a cleaner gradient.
  • Near the solution, noise matters more than cost, so growing the batch over time is an alternative to shrinking the step (§10).

9.1Why is the mini-batch gradient unbiased when the batch is drawn without replacement?

Each index is in the batch with probability b/nb/nb/n, so E[1b∑i∈B∇ℓi]=1b⋅bn∑i∇ℓi=∇F\E[\frac1b\sum_{i\in\cB}\nabla\ell_i]=\frac1b\cdot\frac bn\sum_i\nabla\ell_i=\nabla FE[b1​∑i∈B​∇ℓi​]=b1​⋅nb​∑i​∇ℓi​=∇F.

9.3What does mini-batch SGD become for b=nb=nb=n without replacement?

The batch is the whole dataset, so gt=∇F(β(t))\bg_t=\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})gt​=∇F(β(t)) exactly: full gradient descent, with zero noise (consistent with the factor n−bn−1=0\frac{n-b}{n-1}=0n−1n−b​=0).

§10Slides pp. 37–40

Choosing the learning rate

A constant step makes fast progress and then stalls in the noise ball. A step that shrinks neither too fast nor too slowly lets the noise average out: the Robbins–Monro conditions say exactly how fast.

What the learning rate controls

SGD updates β(t+1)=β(t)−γtgt\bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma_t\bg_tβ(t+1)=β(t)−γt​gt​. The learning rate γt>0\gamma_t>0γt​>0 controls both progress (how far the iterate moves along the signal ∇F\nabla F∇F) and sensitivity to gradient noise (how far it is kicked by the noise ξt\bxi_tξt​). Both scale with γt\gamma_tγt​: there is no way to get the first without the second, except by changing γt\gamma_tγt​ over time.

Constant learning rate γt=γ\gamma_t=\gammaγt​=γ

  • allows fast initial progress;
  • but stochastic fluctuations generally persist near a solution (slide p. 38).

This is the noise ball of §8: the error forgets its initial value geometrically, then plateaus at a level proportional to γ\gammaγ. A constant step is the right choice when a rough solution is enough, or when the problem keeps changing (online learning), so that the ability to keep adapting matters more than precision.

Decreasing learning rate

Slide p. 39 · power-law schedule

γt=C(t+t0)α.\displaystyle \gamma_t=\frac{C}{(t+t_0)^\alpha}.γt​=(t+t0​)αC​.

CCC sets the scale, t0≥1t_0\ge1t0​≥1 delays the decay (it avoids dividing by zero at t=0t=0t=0, and a larger t0t_0t0​ keeps the first steps from being huge), and α\alphaα sets the speed of decay. Under standard assumptions (convexity, unbiased gradients with bounded variance), the classical stochastic-approximation conditions (Robbins and Monro, 1951) are

Slide p. 39

∑t=0∞γt=∞,∑t=0∞γt2<∞.\displaystyle {\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma_t=\infty,}\qquad\allowbreak { \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma_t^2<\infty.}t=0∑∞​γt​=∞,t=0∑∞​γt2​<∞.
  • ∑γt=∞\sum\gamma_t=\infty∑γt​=∞: the steps must not die out too early. The total distance SGD can travel is at most about G∑γtG\sum\gamma_tG∑γt​. If this sum is finite, the iterates may stop before reaching the solution; in the mean example the initial error is multiplied by ∏k(1−γk)\prod_k(1-\gamma_k)∏k​(1−γk​), which tends to 0 only if ∑γk=∞\sum\gamma_k=\infty∑γk​=∞.
  • ∑γt2<∞\sum\gamma_t^2<\infty∑γt2​<∞: the total injected noise is finite. Step ttt injects noise γtξt\gamma_t\bxi_tγt​ξt​ with variance γt2σ2\gamma_t^2\sigma^2γt2​σ2; when these variances are summable, the accumulated zero-mean noise converges instead of building up like a random walk. This is what the classical (almost-sure) convergence proof uses, and it is sufficient rather than necessary: under strong convexity the contraction of the error also damps old noise, so any γt→0\gamma_t\to0γt​→0 with ∑γt=∞{\sum\gamma_t=\infty}∑γt​=∞ makes the mean squared error vanish, roughly like γt\gamma_tγt​. With α≤12\alpha\le\tfrac12α≤21​ the noise ball still shrinks, only more slowly.

For power-law schedules this corresponds to

Slide p. 39

12<α≤1.\displaystyle \frac12<\alpha\le1.21​<α≤1.

Derivation

By the integral test, ∑tt−p\sum_tt^{-p}∑t​t−p converges iff p>1p>1p>1. The first condition needs ∑t(t+t0)−α=∞\sum_t(t+t_0)^{-\alpha}=\infty∑t​(t+t0​)−α=∞, i.e. α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1. The second needs ∑t(t+t0)−2α<∞\sum_t(t+t_0)^{-2\alpha}<\infty∑t​(t+t0​)−2α<∞, i.e. 2α>12\alpha>12α>1.

Watch out Beyond the slides

  • The constant CCC matters for α=1\alpha=1α=1. For a μ\muμ-strongly convex objective, γt=C/t\gamma_t=C/tγt​=C/t gives the optimal error decrease in O(1/t)O(1/t)O(1/t) only if CCC is large enough (C>12μC>\frac1{2\mu}C>2μ1​); with a smaller CCC the decrease can be dramatically slower. Underestimating μ\muμ is safer than overestimating it.
  • Too large a first step diverges. Whatever the schedule, the early steps should respect the deterministic stability limit (γ≲1/L\gamma\lesssim1/Lγ≲1/L); that is what t0t_0t0​ is for.
  • The conditions are sufficient, not a recipe. Deep learning commonly uses piecewise-constant schedules (divide by 10 at fixed epochs), a short warm-up followed by linear or cosine decay, or "reduce when the validation loss plateaus". They all follow the same principle.

Averaging the iterates Beyond the slides

The take-home slide lists "learning-rate schedules and averaging" as ways to control the noise. Polyak–Ruppert averaging returns, instead of the last iterate, the average

βˉT=1T∑t=1Tβ(t).\displaystyle \bar\bbeta_T=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\bbeta^{(t)}.βˉ​T​=T1​t=1∑T​β(t).

The iterates fluctuate around β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ in a correlated way; averaging cancels much of that noise. Combined with steps that decrease more slowly than 1/t1/t1/t (for instance α\alphaα between 12\tfrac1221​ and 1), averaging achieves the best possible rate and is far less sensitive to the choice of CCC than the last iterate with γt=C/t\gamma_t=C/tγt​=C/t.

Worked example D · Averaging a constant-step run

In the mean example with a constant step, et+1=(1−γ)et+γηte_{t+1}=(1-\gamma)e_t+\gamma\eta_tet+1​=(1−γ)et​+γηt​ with independent noise ηt\eta_tηt​ of variance s2s^2s2. For large TTT, the variance of 1T∑tet\frac1T\sum_te_tT1​∑t​et​ is approximately 1T\frac1TT1​ times the "long-run variance" of the process, which for this recursion is γ2s2(1−(1−γ))2=s2\frac{\gamma^2s^2}{(1-(1-\gamma))^2}=s^2(1−(1−γ))2γ2s2​=s2. Hence Var⁡(βˉT)≈s2/T\Var(\bar\beta_T)\approx s^2/TVar(βˉ​T​)≈s2/T: whatever the constant step, the average of the iterates ends up as accurate as the sample mean, even though each iterate keeps fluctuating with variance γs2/(2−γ)\gamma s^2/(2-\gamma)γs2/(2−γ). §11Slides pp. 41–43

SGD with momentum

SGD directions can change a lot from one step to the next. Momentum keeps a running memory of past steps: components that persist add up, components that oscillate cancel out.

The update

SGD directions can fluctuate strongly from one iteration to the next (slide p. 41). Momentum accumulates information from previous updates in a velocity v(t)\bv^{(t)}v(t):

Slide p. 41 · SGD with momentum

v(t+1)=θ v(t)−γt gt,β(t+1)=β(t)+v(t+1),θ∈[0,1).\displaystyle {\bv^{(t+1)}=\theta\,\bv^{(t)}-\gamma_t\,\bg_t,}\qquad\allowbreak { \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}+\bv^{(t+1)},}\qquad\allowbreak { \theta\in[0,1).}v(t+1)=θv(t)−γt​gt​,β(t+1)=β(t)+v(t+1),θ∈[0,1).

Start with v(0)=0\bv^{(0)}=\bzerov(0)=0. Each step first shrinks the previous velocity by the factor θ\thetaθ (typically 0.90.90.9), then adds the usual SGD step −γtgt-\gamma_t\bg_t−γt​gt​, and moves by the result. The physical picture is a heavy ball rolling on the graph of FFF: the gradient is the force, the velocity carries the ball through small bumps, and 1−θ1-\theta1−θ plays the role of friction. The restriction θ<1\theta<1θ<1 matters: with θ=1\theta=1θ=1 there is no friction, old gradients never fade, and under a constant gradient the velocity grows without bound.

An exponentially weighted memory

Derivation · unrolling the velocity

Apply the recursion repeatedly, starting from v(0)=0\bv^{(0)}=\bzerov(0)=0: v(1)=−γ0g0\bv^{(1)}=-\gamma_0\bg_0v(1)=−γ0​g0​, v(2)=−θγ0g0−γ1g1\bv^{(2)}=-\theta\gamma_0\bg_0-\gamma_1\bg_1v(2)=−θγ0​g0​−γ1​g1​, and by induction

v(t+1)=−∑k=0tθ t−kγk gk,soβ(t+1)=β(t)−(γtgt+θγt−1gt−1+θ2γt−2gt−2+⋯).\displaystyle {\bv^{(t+1)}=-\sum_{k=0}^{t}\theta^{\,t-k}\gamma_k\,\bg_k,}\qquad\allowbreak {\text{so}}\qquad\allowbreak \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\Big(\gamma_t\bg_t+\theta\gamma_{t-1}\bg_{t-1}+\allowbreak\theta^2\gamma_{t-2}\bg_{t-2}+\cdots\Big).v(t+1)=−k=0∑t​θt−kγk​gk​,soβ(t+1)=β(t)−(γt​gt​+θγt−1​gt−1​+θ2γt−2​gt−2​+⋯).
∎

Each step moves along a weighted sum of all past stochastic gradients: weight 1 for the newest, θ\thetaθ for the previous one, θ2\theta^2θ2 for the one before, and so on.

In the words of slide p. 42, the velocity v(t)\bv^{(t)}v(t) acts as an exponentially weighted memory of past stochastic gradients.

With θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9 the weights halve every log⁡2/log⁡(1/θ)≈6.6\log2/\log(1/\theta)\approx6.6log2/log(1/θ)≈6.6 steps, and they sum to 1/(1−θ)=101/(1-\theta)=101/(1−θ)=10: the memory spans roughly the last ten gradients. For θ=0\theta=0θ=0 the memory is empty, v(t+1)=−γtgt\bv^{(t+1)}=-\gamma_t\bg_tv(t+1)=−γt​gt​, and we recover standard SGD (slide p. 43).

The heavy-ball form Beyond the slides

Since v(t)=β(t)−β(t−1)\bv^{(t)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\bbeta^{(t-1)}v(t)=β(t)−β(t−1), the velocity can be eliminated:

β(t+1)=β(t)−γt gt+θ (β(t)−β(t−1)).\displaystyle \bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma_t\,\bg_t+\theta\,\big(\bbeta^{(t)}-\bbeta^{(t-1)}\big).β(t+1)=β(t)−γt​gt​+θ(β(t)−β(t−1)).

An SGD step plus a fraction θ\thetaθ of the previous displacement. This is Polyak's heavy-ball method (1964). Deep-learning libraries store v\bvv differently (PyTorch keeps v←θv+g\bv\leftarrow\theta\bv+\bgv←θv+g and steps by −γv-\gamma\bv−γv), which is the same algorithm for a constant γ\gammaγ.

Reinforce what persists, cancel what oscillates

Slide p. 42 lists three consequences of the memory:

  • directions that persist across iterations are reinforced;
  • rapidly oscillating directions tend to compensate;
  • progress can be faster along directions of consistent descent.

The two extreme cases make this quantitative (constant γ\gammaγ, one coordinate):

Derivation · constant and alternating gradients

  1. Constant gradient ggg. The velocity satisfies vt+1=θvt−γgv_{t+1}=\theta v_t-\gamma gvt+1​=θvt​−γg, whose fixed point is v∞=−γ1−θ gv_\infty=-\dfrac{\gamma}{1-\theta}\,gv∞​=−1−θγ​g. The ball reaches a terminal speed 1/(1−θ)1/(1-\theta)1/(1−θ) times larger than a plain SGD step.
  2. Alternating gradient +g,−g,+g,…+g,-g,+g,\dots+g,−g,+g,… Over two consecutive steps (first +g+g+g, then −g-g−g), vt+1=θvt−γgv_{t+1}=\theta v_t-\gamma gvt+1​=θvt​−γg and vt+2=θvt+1+γg=θ2vt+(1−θ)γgv_{t+2}=\theta v_{t+1}+\gamma g=\theta^2v_t+(1-\theta)\gamma gvt+2​=θvt+1​+γg=θ2vt​+(1−θ)γg. The fixed point is v=(1−θ)γg1−θ2=γg1+θv=\dfrac{(1-\theta)\gamma g}{1-\theta^2}=\dfrac{\gamma g}{1+\theta}v=1−θ2(1−θ)γg​=1+θγg​, and the step in between gives −γg1+θ-\dfrac{\gamma g}{1+\theta}−1+θγg​. The velocity settles into an oscillation of amplitude γ1+θ∣g∣\dfrac{\gamma}{1+\theta}\abs g1+θγ​∣g∣: damped by the factor 1+θ1+\theta1+θ compared with SGD.
  3. So momentum multiplies persistent components by 11−θ\frac1{1-\theta}1−θ1​ and oscillating ones by 11+θ\frac1{1+\theta}1+θ1​: a relative amplification of 1+θ1−θ\frac{1+\theta}{1-\theta}1−θ1+θ​, which is 191919 for θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9.
∎

Intuition · signal and noise in the velocity

Write gt=∇F(β(t))+ξt\bg_t=\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})+\bxi_tgt​=∇F(β(t))+ξt​ (§8), and suppose that over a stretch of iterations ∇F\nabla F∇F barely changes while the noise terms are independent with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. In the velocity the signal is a "constant gradient": it builds up to γ∥∇F∥/(1−θ)\gamma\norm{\nabla F}/(1-\theta)γ∥∇F∥/(1−θ). The noise partly cancels: its contribution has variance γ2σ2∑kθ2k=γ2σ2/(1−θ2)\gamma^2\sigma^2\sum_k\theta^{2k}=\gamma^2\sigma^2/(1-\theta^2)γ2σ2∑k​θ2k=γ2σ2/(1−θ2). Relative to a single stochastic gradient, the signal-to-noise ratio of each step improves by 1/(1−θ)1/1−θ2=1+θ1−θ\frac{1/(1-\theta)}{1/\sqrt{1-\theta^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+\theta}{1-\theta}}1/1−θ2​1/(1−θ)​=1−θ1+θ​​, about 4.44.44.4 for θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9. The direction actually followed is a smoothed version of the stochastic gradients: less zig-zag.

Momentum in narrow valleys Beyond the slides

Momentum is older than SGD-for-machine-learning: it was invented to speed up deterministic gradient descent on ill-conditioned problems. Take F(β)=12(μβ12+Lβ22)F(\bbeta)=\tfrac12(\mu\beta_1^2+L\beta_2^2)F(β)=21​(μβ12​+Lβ22​) with κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\muκ=L/μ. Along β2\beta_2β2​ (steep) gradient descent overshoots and the gradient flips sign at every step: momentum damps it. Along β1\beta_1β1​ (flat) the gradient keeps the same sign: momentum accelerates. With tuned constants γ=4(L+μ)2\gamma=\frac4{(\sqrt L+\sqrt\mu)^2}γ=(L​+μ​)24​ and θ=(κ−1κ+1)2\theta=\big(\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}\big)^2θ=(κ​+1κ​−1​)2, the error contracts per step by

κ−1κ+1⏟gradient descent, best γversusκ−1κ+1⏟heavy ball.\displaystyle \underbrace{\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}}_{\text{gradient descent, best }\gamma}\qquad\allowbreak {\text{versus}}\qquad\allowbreak {\underbrace{\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}}_{\text{heavy ball}}.}gradient descent, best γκ+1κ−1​​​versusheavy ballκ​+1κ​−1​​​.

For κ=100\kappa=100κ=100: 0.9800.9800.980 versus 0.8180.8180.818. To divide the error by 10610^6106, gradient descent needs 691 iterations and the heavy ball 93 in a simulation (the asymptotic rate predicts 69; there is a transient). The number of iterations scales like κ\kappaκ for gradient descent and like κ\sqrt\kappaκ​ with momentum. Nesterov's variant, which evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point β(t)+θv(t)\bbeta^{(t)}+\theta\bv^{(t)}β(t)+θv(t), guarantees this κ\sqrt\kappaκ​ behaviour for every smooth strongly convex function (and an O(1/t2)O(1/t^2)O(1/t2) rate instead of O(1/t)O(1/t)O(1/t) for smooth convex ones), whereas for the heavy ball it is only guaranteed on quadratics and close to a minimizer.

Watch out Beyond the slides

  • The effective step is γ/(1−θ)\gamma/(1-\theta)γ/(1−θ). Adding θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9 to a tuned SGD multiplies the step along persistent directions by 10. To keep a comparable behaviour, divide γ\gammaγ by about 1/(1−θ)1/(1-\theta)1/(1−θ).
  • Smoother is not the same as more accurate. Consecutive momentum steps share the same past noise, so over the length of the memory the noise accumulates much as in plain SGD with step γ/(1−θ)\gamma/(1-\theta)γ/(1−θ). With small constant steps, SGD with momentum ends in the same kind of noise ball as that SGD. Its decisive advantage is on ill-conditioned problems; to converge you still need decreasing steps, averaging (§10) or variance reduction (§13).
  • On a quadratic, the heavy ball is stable for 0<γλ<2(1+θ)0<\gamma\lambda<2(1+\theta)0<γλ<2(1+θ) along a direction of curvature λ\lambdaλ, but with θ\thetaθ close to 1 the iterates overshoot and spiral before settling: momentum makes the path non-monotone even without noise.
SGD with momentum
import numpy as np

def sgd_momentum(grad_i, beta0, n, n_steps, gamma=0.01, theta=0.9, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta, v = beta0.copy(), np.zeros_like(beta0)
    for t in range(n_steps):
        g = grad_i(beta, rng.integers(n))       # stochastic gradient g_t
        v = theta * v - gamma * g                # velocity: decaying sum of past steps
        beta = beta + v                          # theta = 0 gives plain SGD
    return beta

Momentum introduces memory into the stochastic update.

Check yourself

11.1Write v(3)\bv^{(3)}v(3) in terms of g0,g1,g2\bg_0,\bg_1,\bg_2g0​,g1​,g2​. What happens when θ=0\theta=0θ=0?

v(3)=−(θ2γ0g0+θγ1g1+γ2g2)\bv^{(3)}=-(\theta^2\gamma_0\bg_0+\theta\gamma_1\bg_1+\gamma_2\bg_2)v(3)=−(θ2γ0​g0​+θγ1​g1​+γ2​g2​). With θ=0\theta=0θ=0 only −γ2g2-\gamma_2\bg_2−γ2​g2​ remains: the update is plain SGD.

11.2With θ=0.99\theta=0.99θ=0.99, what is the terminal velocity under a constant gradient, and how long is the memory?

−γg/(1−0.99)=−100 γg-\gamma g/(1-0.99)=-100\,\gamma g−γg/(1−0.99)=−100γg: a hundred times the SGD step. The weights sum to 100 and halve every log⁡2/log⁡(1/0.99)≈69\log2/\log(1/0.99)\approx69log2/log(1/0.99)≈69 steps, so the memory covers on the order of 100 steps.

11.3Derive the heavy-ball form from the two-line update.

From β(t)=β(t−1)+v(t)\bbeta^{(t)}=\bbeta^{(t-1)}+\bv^{(t)}β(t)=β(t−1)+v(t) we get v(t)=β(t)−β(t−1)\bv^{(t)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\bbeta^{(t-1)}v(t)=β(t)−β(t−1). Substitute into β(t+1)=β(t)+θv(t)−γtgt\bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}+\theta\bv^{(t)}-\gamma_t\bg_tβ(t+1)=β(t)+θv(t)−γt​gt​.

11.4Why does momentum help on a narrow valley even without noise?

Across the valley the gradient flips sign at each step, so those components cancel in the velocity (damping by 1+θ1+\theta1+θ); along the valley it keeps its sign, so the velocity builds up (amplification by 1/(1−θ)1/(1-\theta)1/(1−θ)). The method can then use a step that is stable across the valley and still move fast along it: iterations scale like κ\sqrt\kappaκ​ instead of κ\kappaκ.

§12Slides pp. 44–51

Adaptive learning rates: AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam

A single learning rate is a compromise: too large for the coordinates with large gradients, too small for those with small ones. Adaptive methods give every coordinate its own step size, computed from the history of its own gradients.

One step size does not fit all coordinates

A single learning rate γt\gamma_tγt​ treats all coordinates identically. But different parameters may experience gradients with very different magnitudes (slide p. 44). Typical reasons:

  • Feature scales. ∂ℓi/∂βj\partial\ell_i/\partial\beta_j∂ℓi​/∂βj​ is proportional to xijx_{ij}xij​ (§4: ∇ℓi=−σ(−mi)yixi\nabla\ell_i=-\sigma(-m_i)y_i\bx_i∇ℓi​=−σ(−mi​)yi​xi​). A feature measured in grams instead of kilograms has gradients a thousand times larger.
  • Sparse features. In a bag-of-words model, the coefficient of a rare word receives a nonzero gradient only for the few documents that contain it.
  • Curvature. As in §4 and §11, the step must be small enough for the steepest direction (γ<2/L\gamma<2/Lγ<2/L), and then the flattest directions crawl: the condition number κ\kappaκ sets the speed.

Standardizing the features (Course II) is the manual fix. The methods of this section find a per-coordinate scaling automatically, from the gradients themselves.

AdaGrad

In this section, as on the slides, g(t)\bg^{(t)}g(t) denotes the stochastic gradient used at step ttt (the gt\bg_tgt​ of §7–§11) and gj(t)g^{(t)}_jgj(t)​ its jjj-th coordinate; steps are counted from t=1t=1t=1. AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan and Singer, 2011) accumulates the squared stochastic gradients of each coordinate and divides by their square root:

Slide p. 45 · AdaGrad

sj(t)=∑k=1t(gj(k))2,βj(t+1)=βj(t)−γsj(t)+ε gj(t).\displaystyle {s_j^{(t)}=\sum_{k=1}^t\big(g_j^{(k)}\big)^2,}\qquad\allowbreak \beta_j^{(t+1)}=\beta_j^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{s_j^{(t)}}+\varepsilon}\,g_j^{(t)}.sj(t)​=k=1∑t​(gj(k)​)2,βj(t+1)​=βj(t)​−sj(t)​​+εγ​gj(t)​.

The update is performed coordinatewise, and ε\varepsilonε (say 10−810^{-8}10−8) only prevents a division by zero for coordinates that have not received any gradient yet. Thus each coordinate has its own effective learning rate:

Slide p. 46

γj,teff=γsj(t)+ε.\displaystyle \gamma^{\text{eff}}_{j,t}=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{s_j^{(t)}}+\varepsilon}.γj,teff​=sj(t)​​+εγ​.
  • frequently large gradients ⟹ smaller future steps: sjs_jsj​ grows fast, so γj,teff\gamma^{\text{eff}}_{j,t}γj,teff​ shrinks fast;
  • rarely updated coordinates retain comparatively larger steps: their sjs_jsj​ grows slowly.

In matrix form, β(t+1)=β(t)−γ (Dt1/2+εI)−1g(t)\bbeta^{(t+1)}=\bbeta^{(t)}-\gamma\,\big(\bD_t^{1/2}+\varepsilon\bI\big)^{-1}\bg^{(t)}β(t+1)=β(t)−γ(Dt1/2​+εI)−1g(t) with Dt=Diag⁡(sj(t))j\bD_t=\Diag\big(s^{(t)}_j\big)_jDt​=Diag(sj(t)​)j​: a gradient step preconditioned by a diagonal matrix. Newton's method (§4) rescales the gradient by the inverse Hessian; AdaGrad rescales each coordinate by a scale estimated from past gradients alone, at the cost of one extra vector of memory.

AdaGrad adapts the geometry of the update using past gradients.

Derivation · four properties (take ε≈0\varepsilon\approx0ε≈0)

  1. Scale invariance. If every gradient of coordinate jjj is multiplied by c>0c>0c>0, then sjs_jsj​ is multiplied by c2c^2c2 and sj\sqrt{s_j}sj​​ by ccc, so the update γgj/sj\gamma g_j/\sqrt{s_j}γgj​/sj​​ is unchanged. The step of a coordinate no longer depends on the size of its gradients, only on their pattern over time.
  2. The first step is a sign step. At t=1t=1t=1, sj(1)=(gj(1))2s_j^{(1)}=(g_j^{(1)})^2sj(1)​=(gj(1)​)2, so βj(2)−βj(1)=−γ gj(1)/∣gj(1)∣=−γsign⁡(gj(1))\beta_j^{(2)}-\beta_j^{(1)}=-\gamma\,g_j^{(1)}/\abs{g_j^{(1)}}=-\gamma\sign(g_j^{(1)})βj(2)​−βj(1)​=−γgj(1)​/​gj(1)​​=−γsign(gj(1)​): every coordinate with a nonzero gradient moves by exactly γ\gammaγ.
  3. A built-in 1/t1/\sqrt t1/t​ schedule. If ∣gj(k)∣≈G\abs{g_j^{(k)}}\approx G​gj(k)​​≈G at every step, sj(t)≈tG2s_j^{(t)}\approx tG^2sj(t)​≈tG2 and γj,teff≈γ/(Gt)\gamma^{\text{eff}}_{j,t}\approx\gamma/(G\sqrt t)γj,teff​≈γ/(Gt​): the effective step is divided by 10 after 100 steps and by 1000 after a million.
  4. Rare coordinates. If coordinate 222 receives a gradient of the same size as coordinate 111 but only one step in ten, then after 100 steps s1=100G2s_1=100G^2s1​=100G2 and s2=10G2s_2=10G^2s2​=10G2: coordinate 2 keeps a step 10≈3.2\sqrt{10}\approx3.210​≈3.2 times larger.
∎

From then on the two effective steps differ by exactly the factor 100100100, the ratio of the curvatures, so both coordinates shrink together, by a factor of about 0.570.570.57 per step. AdaGrad needs 13 iterations to get both below 10−310^{-3}10−3. It found the ideal diagonal preconditioner Diag⁡(100,1)−1\Diag(100,1)^{-1}Diag(100,1)−1 from gradients alone. This is a best case: a diagonal scaling cannot undo ill-conditioning along directions that are not coordinate axes (correlated features), where the gain is smaller.

From AdaGrad to RMSProp

Since sj(t)s_j^{(t)}sj(t)​ keeps increasing, the effective learning rates may eventually become very small (slide p. 48). For a convex problem that is fine, even desirable (decreasing steps, §10). For a long training run on a nonconvex model, AdaGrad tends to stop learning too early: after 10610^6106 steps with gradients of size one, the effective step is γ/1000\gamma/1000γ/1000, whatever happens next. RMSProp (Tieleman and Hinton, 2012) replaces the cumulative sum by an exponential moving average:

Slide p. 49 · RMSProp

sj(t)=ρ sj(t−1)+(1−ρ)(gj(t))2,βj(t+1)=βj(t)−γsj(t)+ε gj(t).\displaystyle {s_j^{(t)}=\rho\,s_j^{(t-1)}+(1-\rho)\big(g_j^{(t)}\big)^2,}\qquad\allowbreak \beta_j^{(t+1)}=\beta_j^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{s_j^{(t)}}+\varepsilon}\,g_j^{(t)}.sj(t)​=ρsj(t−1)​+(1−ρ)(gj(t)​)2,βj(t+1)​=βj(t)​−sj(t)​​+εγ​gj(t)​.

The update is unchanged; only the memory changes. With ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1)ρ∈[0,1) (typically 0.90.90.9 or 0.990.990.99), sjs_jsj​ is a weighted mean of the last ≈1/(1−ρ)\approx1/(1-\rho)≈1/(1−ρ) squared gradients (toolkit, §0), so sj\sqrt{s_j}sj​​ is their root mean square, which gives the method its name. The effective step ≈γ/RMS(gj)\approx\gamma/\mathrm{RMS}(g_j)≈γ/RMS(gj​) follows the current scale of the gradients instead of decaying forever: if ∣gj∣≈G\abs{g_j}\approx G∣gj​∣≈G steadily, sj→G2s_j\to G^2sj​→G2 and every step has size about γ\gammaγ.

One flaw remains. Starting from sj(0)=0s_j^{(0)}=0sj(0)​=0, the first average is sj(1)=(1−ρ)(gj(1))2s_j^{(1)}=(1-\rho)(g_j^{(1)})^2sj(1)​=(1−ρ)(gj(1)​)2, far too small, so the first step has size γ/1−ρ\gamma/\sqrt{1-\rho}γ/1−ρ​: 3.2γ3.2\gamma3.2γ for ρ=0.9\rho=0.9ρ=0.9, 10γ10\gamma10γ for ρ=0.99\rho=0.99ρ=0.99. Adam corrects this.

Adam

Adam combines two ideas (slide p. 50):

momentum+adaptive coordinate-wise scaling.\displaystyle {\text{momentum}}\quad\allowbreak {+}\quad\allowbreak {\text{adaptive coordinate-wise scaling.}}momentum+adaptive coordinate-wise scaling.

It maintains exponential moving averages of both gradients (direction, as in momentum) and squared gradients (scale, as in RMSProp). The slides stop here; the precise algorithm (Kingma and Ba, 2015) is Beyond the slides, written with this course's letters (θ\thetaθ for the gradient memory as in §11, ρ\rhoρ for the squared-gradient memory as in RMSProp):

mj(t)=θ mj(t−1)+(1−θ) gj(t),sj(t)=ρ sj(t−1)+(1−ρ)(gj(t))2,\displaystyle {m_j^{(t)}=\theta\,m_j^{(t-1)}+(1-\theta)\,g_j^{(t)},}\qquad\allowbreak { s_j^{(t)}=\rho\,s_j^{(t-1)}+(1-\rho)\big(g_j^{(t)}\big)^2,}mj(t)​=θmj(t−1)​+(1−θ)gj(t)​,sj(t)​=ρsj(t−1)​+(1−ρ)(gj(t)​)2,
m^j(t)=mj(t)1−θt,s^j(t)=sj(t)1−ρt,βj(t+1)=βj(t)−γ m^j(t)s^j(t)+ε.\displaystyle {\widehat m_j^{(t)}=\frac{m_j^{(t)}}{1-\theta^t},}\qquad\allowbreak { \widehat s_j^{(t)}=\frac{s_j^{(t)}}{1-\rho^t},}\qquad\allowbreak \beta_j^{(t+1)}=\beta_j^{(t)}-\gamma\,\frac{\widehat m_j^{(t)}}{\sqrt{\widehat s_j^{(t)}}+\varepsilon}.mj(t)​=1−θtmj(t)​​,sj(t)​=1−ρtsj(t)​​,βj(t+1)​=βj(t)​−γsj(t)​​+εmj(t)​​.

Both averages start at zero. Unrolling, mj(t)=(1−θ)∑k=1tθt−kgj(k)m_j^{(t)}=(1-\theta)\sum_{k=1}^t\theta^{t-k}g_j^{(k)}mj(t)​=(1−θ)∑k=1t​θt−kgj(k)​. If the gradients have a common mean E[gj(k)]=μj\E[g_j^{(k)}]=\mu_jE[gj(k)​]=μj​, then

E[mj(t)]=(1−θ) μj∑k=1tθt−k=(1−θ) μj 1−θt1−θ=(1−θt) μj.\displaystyle \E\big[m_j^{(t)}\big]=(1-\theta)\,\mu_j\sum_{k=1}^t\theta^{t-k}=(1-\theta)\,\mu_j\,\frac{1-\theta^t}{1-\theta}=(1-\theta^t)\,\mu_j.E[mj(t)​]=(1−θ)μj​k=1∑t​θt−k=(1−θ)μj​1−θ1−θt​=(1−θt)μj​.

Intuition · Adam's step is a signal-to-noise ratio

For a coordinate whose stochastic gradients fluctuate around a mean, m^j≈E[gj]\widehat m_j\approx\E[g_j]mj​≈E[gj​] and s^j≈E[gj2]=(Egj)2+Var⁡(gj)\widehat s_j\approx\E[g_j^2]=(\E g_j)^2+\Var(g_j)sj​≈E[gj2​]=(Egj​)2+Var(gj​). The step is therefore about

γ ∣Egj∣(Egj)2+Var⁡(gj) ≤ γ.\displaystyle \gamma\,\frac{\abs{\E g_j}}{\sqrt{(\E g_j)^2+\Var(g_j)}}\ \le\ \gamma.γ(Egj​)2+Var(gj​)​∣Egj​∣​ ≤ γ.
  • Consistent gradient (no noise): step ≈γ\approx\gamma≈γ, whatever the gradient's magnitude.
  • Pure noise (Egj=0\E g_j=0Egj​=0): steps average out to about zero.
  • Mean 0.20.20.2, standard deviation 111: step ≈γ⋅0.2/1.04≈0.196γ\approx\gamma\cdot0.2/\sqrt{1.04}\approx0.196\gamma≈γ⋅0.2/1.04​≈0.196γ (a simulation gives 0.192γ0.192\gamma0.192γ).

So γ\gammaγ is roughly the largest distance a coordinate can move per step, in parameter units. Kingma and Ba bound it by γ(1−θ)/1−ρ≈3.2γ\gamma(1-\theta)/\sqrt{1-\rho}\approx3.2\gammaγ(1−θ)/1−ρ​≈3.2γ in the worst case of a sudden gradient after a long quiet period; in typical situations it stays below γ\gammaγ.
