Watch out Beyond the slides

  • Adaptive does not mean convergent. With a constant γ\gammaγ, RMSProp and Adam keep steps of size about γ\gammaγ and end up in a noise ball, like SGD. In practice they are combined with a learning-rate schedule (warm-up, then decay). There are even convex examples where Adam with its default constants fails to converge (Reddi, Kale and Kumar, 2018).
  • Ridge with Adam is not weight decay. Adding λβ\lambda\bbetaλβ to the gradient gets rescaled by 1/s^j1/\sqrt{\widehat s_j}1/sj​​, so coordinates with large gradients are barely regularized. AdamW applies the decay separately, β←β−γλβ−γm^/(s^+ε)\bbeta\leftarrow\bbeta-\gamma\lambda\bbeta-\gamma\widehat\bmm/(\sqrt{\widehat\bs}+\varepsilon)β←β−γλβ−γm/(s​+ε), and is the usual choice.
  • No universal winner. Adam is often the fastest way to a low training loss with little tuning, and the default for transformers. On some tasks, image classification with convolutional networks for example, well-tuned SGD with momentum has been reported to generalize slightly better.
Adam (theta = 0 and no correction of s gives RMSProp)
import numpy as np

def adam(grad, beta0, n_steps, gamma=1e-3, theta=0.9, rho=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    beta = beta0.copy(); m = np.zeros_like(beta); s = np.zeros_like(beta)
    for t in range(1, n_steps + 1):
        g = grad(beta)                                   # stochastic gradient g^(t)
        m = theta * m + (1 - theta) * g                  # memory of gradients (momentum)
        s = rho * s + (1 - rho) * g ** 2                 # memory of squared gradients (RMSProp)
        m_hat, s_hat = m / (1 - theta ** t), s / (1 - rho ** t)   # bias corrections
        beta -= gamma * m_hat / (np.sqrt(s_hat) + eps)
    return beta

12.4Why may AdaGrad stop making progress in a long nonconvex training run, and how does RMSProp change this?

sjs_jsj​ is a sum of all past squared gradients, so it only grows and the effective step γ/sj\gamma/\sqrt{s_j}γ/sj​​ decays like 1/t1/\sqrt t1/t​ even when the model reaches a new region where larger steps would be useful. RMSProp uses a moving average that forgets old gradients, so the effective step tracks the recent gradient scale.

12.5Which method do you get from Adam with θ=0\theta=0θ=0? Why is AdaGrad called a preconditioned gradient method?

With θ=0\theta=0θ=0, m^=g\widehat m=gm=g and Adam is RMSProp with bias-corrected sss. AdaGrad multiplies the gradient by the diagonal matrix (Dt1/2+εI)−1(\bD_t^{1/2}+\varepsilon\bI)^{-1}(Dt1/2​+εI)−1 before stepping, which is what a preconditioner does; it changes the geometry in which the descent happens.

§13Slides pp. 52–55

Variance reduction: SAG, SAGA, SVRG

SGD's noise does not vanish at the solution, which is why it needs decreasing steps and converges slowly. For a finite sum we can do better: correct each cheap stochastic gradient with gradients we already know, so that the noise disappears as the iterates converge.

Why the noise is the bottleneck

SGD uses a cheap but noisy estimate gt=∇ℓit(β(t))\bg_t=\nabla\ell_{i_t}(\bbeta^{(t)})gt​=∇ℓit​​(β(t)) of the full gradient. Even close to a solution, the individual gradients ∇ℓi(β)\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)∇ℓi​(β) do not necessarily vanish. Thus stochastic gradient noise may persist (slide p. 52). In worked example A, the noise level at the optimum is σ⋆2=16∑i∥∇ℓi(β^)∥2≈0.201\sigma_\star^2=\frac16\sum_i\norm{\nabla\ell_i(\widehat\bbeta)}^2\approx0.201σ⋆2​=61​∑i​​∇ℓi​(β​)​2≈0.201, although ∇F(β^)=0\nabla F(\widehat\bbeta)=\bzero∇F(β​)=0.

The consequences were seen in §8–§10: with a constant step, SGD stalls in a noise ball; with decreasing steps it converges, but slowly. For a strongly convex FFF the error of SGD decreases at best like 1/t1/t1/t, so each additional digit of accuracy costs ten times more iterations, whereas gradient descent gains digits at a constant cost (linear convergence). SGD is unbeatable for a rough solution and hopeless for a precise one.

The idea: subtract what you already know

Variance-reduction idea (slide p. 53): exploit the finite-sum structure

F(β)=1n∑i=1nℓi(β)\displaystyle F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\bbeta)F(β)=n1​i=1∑n​ℓi​(β)

to construct gradient estimates that are

Slide p. 53

cheap+unbiased or controlled+less noisy.\displaystyle {\text{cheap}}\quad\allowbreak {+}\quad\allowbreak {\text{unbiased or controlled}}\quad\allowbreak {+}\quad\allowbreak {\text{less noisy.}}cheap+unbiased or controlled+less noisy.

The tool is a classical trick from Monte Carlo simulation, the control variate Beyond the slides. To estimate E[X]\E[X]E[X], take a random variable YYY that is strongly correlated with XXX and whose mean E[Y]\E[Y]E[Y] you know, and use X−Y+E[Y]X-Y+\E[Y]X−Y+E[Y]. It has the same mean as XXX, and variance Var⁡(X−Y)\Var(X-Y)Var(X−Y), which is small when XXX and YYY move together.

Here X=∇ℓi(β)X=\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)X=∇ℓi​(β) for a random index iii. Take Y=∇ℓi(β~)Y=\nabla\ell_i(\widetilde\bbeta)Y=∇ℓi​(β​), the gradient of the same example at a reference point β~\widetilde\bbetaβ​ where the full gradient ∇F(β~)=Ei[Y]\nabla F(\widetilde\bbeta)=\E_i[Y]∇F(β​)=Ei​[Y] has been computed once:

A variance never exceeds the second moment, so E∥g−∇F(β)∥2≤E∥Z∥2\E\norm{\bg-\nabla F(\bbeta)}^2\le\E\norm{\bZ}^2E∥g−∇F(β)∥2≤E∥Z∥2.

In words: ∇ℓi(β~)−∇F(β~)\nabla\ell_i(\widetilde\bbeta)-\nabla F(\widetilde\bbeta)∇ℓi​(β​)−∇F(β​) measures how atypical example iii is at the reference point, and the estimate subtracts this atypicality from the current gradient of example iii. In the mean example D this works perfectly: ∇ℓi(β)−∇ℓi(β~)=(β−ai)−(β~−ai)=β−β~\nabla\ell_i(\beta)-\nabla\ell_i(\widetilde\beta)=(\beta-a_i)-(\widetilde\beta-a_i)=\beta-\widetilde\beta∇ℓi​(β)−∇ℓi​(β​)=(β−ai​)−(β​−ai​)=β−β​ for every iii, so g=β−β~+β~−aˉ=β−aˉ=∇F(β)g=\beta-\widetilde\beta+\widetilde\beta-\bar a=\beta-\bar a=\nabla F(\beta)g=β−β​+β​−aˉ=β−aˉ=∇F(β) exactly: zero noise, the full gradient at the price of a stochastic one.

Three algorithms

Methods such as SAG, SAGA and SVRG combine stochastic updates with additional information from previous or reference gradients (slide p. 54). They differ in which reference gradients they use and how they store them.

SVRG: a reference point refreshed periodically Details beyond the slides

Stochastic variance-reduced gradient (Johnson and Zhang, 2013) uses one reference point, the snapshot, for many steps:

  1. Snapshot: β~←β\widetilde\bbeta\leftarrow\bbetaβ​←β, and compute the full gradient μ~=∇F(β~)\widetilde\bmu=\nabla F(\widetilde\bbeta)μ​=∇F(β​) (nnn gradient evaluations).
  2. Repeat mmm times (typically mmm of the order of nnn, e.g. 2n2n2n): draw iii uniformly and update β←β−γ(∇ℓi(β)−∇ℓi(β~)+μ~)\bbeta\leftarrow\bbeta-\gamma\big(\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)-\nabla\ell_i(\widetilde\bbeta)+\widetilde\bmu\big)β←β−γ(∇ℓi​(β)−∇ℓi​(β​)+μ​) (2 evaluations each).
  3. Go back to 1.

Memory: two vectors. Cost: a full pass every mmm steps, and two gradients per step.

SAGA: one reference gradient per example Details beyond the slides

SAGA (Defazio, Bach and Lacoste-Julien, 2014) stores, for each example iii, the last gradient computed for it, ϕi\bphi_iϕi​, and their average ϕˉ=1n∑iϕi\bar\bphi=\frac1n\sum_i\bphi_iϕˉ​=n1​∑i​ϕi​. At each step:

  1. draw jjj uniformly and compute ∇ℓj(β)\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta)∇ℓj​(β);
  2. step along g=∇ℓj(β)−ϕj+ϕˉ\bg=\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta)-\bphi_j+\bar\bphig=∇ℓj​(β)−ϕj​+ϕˉ​;
  3. update the memory: ϕˉ←ϕˉ+1n(∇ℓj(β)−ϕj)\bar\bphi\leftarrow\bar\bphi+\frac1n\big(\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta)-\bphi_j\big)ϕˉ​←ϕˉ​+n1​(∇ℓj​(β)−ϕj​), then ϕj←∇ℓj(β)\bphi_j\leftarrow\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta)ϕj​←∇ℓj​(β).

This is the control variate with "the iterate at which example jjj was last visited" as reference point for example jjj. Ej[g]=∇F(β)−ϕˉ+ϕˉ=∇F(β)\E_j[\bg]=\nabla F(\bbeta)-\bar\bphi+\bar\bphi=\nabla F(\bbeta)Ej​[g]=∇F(β)−ϕˉ​+ϕˉ​=∇F(β): unbiased, for any content of the table. One gradient evaluation per step, no full passes, but a table of nnn gradients.

SAG: the averaged version Details beyond the slides

The stochastic average gradient (Le Roux, Schmidt and Bach, 2012), historically the first, uses the same table but steps along the refreshed average: β←β−γ(ϕˉ+1n(∇ℓj(β)−ϕj))\bbeta\leftarrow\bbeta-\gamma\big(\bar\bphi+\frac1n(\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta)-\bphi_j)\big)β←β−γ(ϕˉ​+n1​(∇ℓj​(β)−ϕj​)). The new information enters with weight 1n\frac1nn1​ instead of 1, so the estimate is biased (its expectation is 1n∇F(β)+(1−1n)ϕˉ\frac1n\nabla F(\bbeta)+(1-\frac1n)\bar\bphin1​∇F(β)+(1−n1​)ϕˉ​), but its variance is very small: "controlled" rather than unbiased, in the words of the slide.

Intuition · why a constant step now works

Suppose SAGA's table has been filled at the solution, ϕi=∇ℓi(β⋆)\bphi_i=\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta^\star)ϕi​=∇ℓi​(β⋆) for all iii. At β=β⋆\bbeta=\bbeta^\starβ=β⋆ the estimate is ∇ℓj(β⋆)−∇ℓj(β⋆)+1n∑i∇ℓi(β⋆)=0\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta^\star)-\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta^\star)+\frac1n\sum_i\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta^\star)=\bzero∇ℓj​(β⋆)−∇ℓj​(β⋆)+n1​∑i​∇ℓi​(β⋆)=0, whichever jjj is drawn: the solution is a fixed point, as for gradient descent. For SGD it is not: at β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ it still moves by γ∇ℓj(β⋆)≠0\gamma\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta^\star)\ne\bzeroγ∇ℓj​(β⋆)=0. Nothing pushes the variance-reduced iterates away from β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆, so the step does not need to shrink.

How much is gained Beyond the slides

Let FFF be μ\muμ-strongly convex and every ℓi\ell_iℓi​ be Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​-smooth. With a constant step of order 1/Lmax⁡1/L_{\max}1/Lmax​ (for instance γ=1/(3Lmax⁡)\gamma=1/(3L_{\max})γ=1/(3Lmax​) for SAGA), SAG, SAGA and SVRG converge linearly, and the number of individual gradient evaluations needed to reach accuracy ε\varepsilonε is

O(n Lμ log⁡1ε)⏟gradient descentversusO((n+Lmax⁡μ)log⁡1ε)⏟SAG, SAGA, SVRG,\displaystyle \underbrace{O\Big(n\,\frac L\mu\,\log\frac1\varepsilon\Big)}_{\text{gradient descent}}\qquad\allowbreak {\text{versus}}\qquad\allowbreak \underbrace{O\Big(\big(n+\tfrac{L_{\max}}\mu\big)\log\frac1\varepsilon\Big)}_{\text{SAG, SAGA, SVRG}},gradient descentO(nμL​logε1​)​​versusSAG, SAGA, SVRGO((n+μLmax​​)logε1​)​​,

while SGD needs O(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon)O(1/ε) evaluations. Gradient descent pays the condition number times the data size; variance reduction pays them added. With n=106n=10^6n=106 examples and a condition number of 10310^3103 (and Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​ of the same order as LLL), that is about 10910^9109 versus 10610^6106 evaluations per factor eee of accuracy.

SGD reduces the cost of each iteration; variance-reduced methods also try to recover the accuracy of full gradient descent.

Watch out Beyond the slides

  • Memory. SAG and SAGA store nnn gradients, i.e. n×(d+1)n\times(d+1)n×(d+1) numbers in general. For linear models the gradient is ∇ℓi=ci xi\nabla\ell_i=c_i\,\bx_i∇ℓi​=ci​xi​ with a scalar cic_ici​ (for logistic regression ci=−yiσ(−mi)c_i=-y_i\sigma(-m_i)ci​=−yi​σ(−mi​)), so storing the nnn scalars cic_ici​ is enough: that is how scikit-learn's sag and saga solvers work.
  • The step is set by Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​, the smoothness of the worst single example, not by LLL. One example with a huge ∥xi∥\norm{\bx_i}∥xi​∥ forces tiny steps: scale your features.
  • Where they do not help. With streaming data (each example seen once) there is no finite sum to exploit. In deep learning, variance reduction rarely beats well-tuned SGD or Adam: the problems are nonconvex, data augmentation changes the examples at every epoch, and moderate accuracy is enough.
SVRG for any finite sum
import numpy as np

def svrg(grad_i, full_grad, beta0, n, n_outer, m, gamma, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta = beta0.copy()
    for _ in range(n_outer):
        snap, mu = beta.copy(), full_grad(beta)            # reference point and its full gradient
        for _ in range(m):
            i = rng.integers(n)
            g = grad_i(beta, i) - grad_i(snap, i) + mu     # unbiased, variance -> 0 near the optimum
            beta -= gamma * g
    return beta
SAGA for logistic regression, storing one scalar per example
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(u):
    return 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(0.5 * u))

def saga_logistic(X, y, gamma, n_epochs, seed=0):
    n = len(y); rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    c = -y * sigmoid(-y * (X @ beta))              # grad l_i = c_i x_i: store one scalar per example
    avg = X.T @ c / n                              # average of the stored gradients
    for _ in range(n_epochs * n):
        j = rng.integers(n)
        c_new = -y[j] * sigmoid(-y[j] * (X[j] @ beta))
        g = (c_new - c[j]) * X[j] + avg            # SAGA direction: unbiased, vanishing variance
        avg += (c_new - c[j]) * X[j] / n
        c[j] = c_new
        beta -= gamma * g
    return beta

# On worked example A with gamma = 1/(3 L_max), 300 epochs give beta = (0, 1.21403): the exact minimizer.

Check yourself

13.1Prove that the SVRG estimate is unbiased. Which quantity must be computed exactly for this to hold?

Ei[∇ℓi(β)−∇ℓi(β~)]=∇F(β)−∇F(β~)\E_i[\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta)-\nabla\ell_i(\widetilde\bbeta)]=\nabla F(\bbeta)-\nabla F(\widetilde\bbeta)Ei​[∇ℓi​(β)−∇ℓi​(β​)]=∇F(β)−∇F(β​), and adding ∇F(β~)\nabla F(\widetilde\bbeta)∇F(β​) gives ∇F(β)\nabla F(\bbeta)∇F(β). It requires the exact full gradient at the snapshot, which is why SVRG pays a full pass for each snapshot.

13.2In the mean example D, show that SVRG's estimate is the exact gradient. What does that say about SVRG on this problem?

(β−ai)−(β~−ai)+(β~−aˉ)=β−aˉ=∇F(β)(\beta-a_i)-(\widetilde\beta-a_i)+(\widetilde\beta-\bar a)=\beta-\bar a=\nabla F(\beta)(β−ai​)−(β​−ai​)+(β​−aˉ)=β−aˉ=∇F(β) for every iii. The noise is exactly zero: SVRG behaves like gradient descent, with one or two gradient evaluations per step instead of nnn.

13.3Why is the minimizer a fixed point of SAGA (once its table is filled there) but not of SGD? Why does that allow a constant step?

At β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆ with ϕi=∇ℓi(β⋆)\bphi_i=\nabla\ell_i(\bbeta^\star)ϕi​=∇ℓi​(β⋆), SAGA's direction is ϕj−ϕj+1n∑iϕi=∇F(β⋆)=0\bphi_j-\bphi_j+\frac1n\sum_i\bphi_i=\nabla F(\bbeta^\star)=\bzeroϕj​−ϕj​+n1​∑i​ϕi​=∇F(β⋆)=0 for every jjj, while SGD's is ∇ℓj(β⋆)≠0\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta^\star)\neq\bzero∇ℓj​(β⋆)=0. Since the estimate's noise vanishes at the solution, the iterates are not kicked out of it, and the step need not decrease.

13.4Logistic regression with n=106n=10^6n=106 examples and d=103d=10^3d=103 features: how much memory does SAGA's table need, naively and with the scalar trick? What does one outer loop of SVRG with m=2nm=2nm=2n cost?

Naively n(d+1)≈109n(d+1)\approx10^9n(d+1)≈109 numbers (8 GB in double precision); with ∇ℓi=cixi\nabla\ell_i=c_i\bx_i∇ℓi​=ci​xi​, 10610^6106 scalars (8 MB). SVRG: nnn evaluations for the snapshot plus 2m=4n2m=4n2m=4n in the inner loop, so 5n5n5n evaluations (5 epochs) per outer loop, with only two extra vectors of memory.

13.5Compute the expectation of SAG's step direction. Why is it biased, and why is that acceptable?

Ej[ϕˉ+1n(∇ℓj(β)−ϕj)]=ϕˉ+1n(∇F(β)−ϕˉ)=1n∇F(β)+(1−1n)ϕˉ\E_j\big[\bar\bphi+\frac1n(\nabla\ell_j(\bbeta)-\bphi_j)\big]=\bar\bphi+\frac1n\big(\nabla F(\bbeta)-\bar\bphi\big)=\frac1n\nabla F(\bbeta)+\big(1-\frac1n\big)\bar\bphiEj​[ϕˉ​+n1​(∇ℓj​(β)−ϕj​)]=ϕˉ​+n1​(∇F(β)−ϕˉ​)=n1​∇F(β)+(1−n1​)ϕˉ​, not ∇F(β)\nabla F(\bbeta)∇F(β). The bias is toward the stored (older) gradients and disappears as the table catches up with the iterates; in exchange the direction changes very little from one step to the next (low variance).

§14Slides pp. 56–58

Take-home messages and cheat sheet

The lecture's closing messages, what each one really says, the main messages of the classification part, and every formula of the lecture on one page.

Stochastic optimization: the take-home messages

For large finite-sum problems F(β)=1n∑i=1nℓi(β)F(\bbeta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\bbeta)F(β)=n1​∑i=1n​ℓi​(β), the main challenge is to balance

Slide p. 56

cost per iterationandaccuracy of the gradient.\displaystyle {\text{cost per iteration}}\qquad\allowbreak {\text{and}}\qquad\allowbreak {\text{accuracy of the gradient.}}cost per iterationandaccuracy of the gradient.
  1. Full gradient descent: accurate direction, but processes the entire dataset. Each step costs O(nd)O(nd)O(nd); with γ≤1/L\gamma\le1/Lγ≤1/L it decreases FFF at every step and converges linearly on strongly convex problems, but the number of steps grows with the condition number (§4, §6).
  2. SGD: cheap iterations using unbiased but noisy gradient estimates. O(d)O(d)O(d) per step, E[gt∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t))\E[\bg_t\mid\bbeta^{(t)}]=\nabla F(\bbeta^{(t)})E[gt​∣β(t)]=∇F(β(t)), but the noise does not vanish at the optimum: fast at first, then stuck in a noise ball of size proportional to γ\gammaγ (§7, §8).
  3. Mini-batches: a compromise between computational cost and gradient variance. Averaging bbb gradients divides the noise variance by bbb and multiplies the cost by bbb; nearly free up to the parallelism of the hardware (§9).
  4. Learning-rate schedules and averaging: control the effect of stochastic noise. ∑γt=∞\sum\gamma_t=\infty∑γt​=∞ and ∑γt2<∞\sum\gamma_t^2<\infty∑γt2​<∞, i.e. γt∝t−α\gamma_t\propto t^{-\alpha}γt​∝t−α with 12<α≤1\tfrac12<\alpha\le121​<α≤1; averaging the iterates cancels the fluctuations (§10).
  5. Momentum: introduces memory of previous directions. Persistent components are amplified by 1/(1−θ)1/(1-\theta)1/(1−θ), oscillating ones damped by 1/(1+θ)1/(1+\theta)1/(1+θ); decisive on ill-conditioned problems (§11).
  6. AdaGrad / RMSProp / Adam: adapt learning rates using past gradients. Each coordinate is divided by the root of its accumulated (AdaGrad) or recent (RMSProp, Adam) squared gradients; Adam adds momentum and bias corrections (§12).
  7. Variance-reduced methods: exploit the finite-sum structure to reduce stochastic noise. Control variates built from stored or reference gradients make the noise vanish at the solution, giving linear convergence at the cost per step of SGD (§13).

There is no universally best optimizer: the appropriate method depends on the structure and scale of the learning problem.

Linear classification: the main messages

The first part of the lecture has no summary slide. These are its main messages in order; the three sentences printed in green on the slides are shown in green.

  1. Classify with the sign of a linear score. The boundary {x⊤β=0}\{\bx\T\bbeta=0\}{x⊤β=0} is a hyperplane and ∣fβ(x)∣/∥w∥\abs{f_{\bbeta}(\bx)}/\norm{\bw}∣fβ​(x)∣/∥w∥ is the distance to it (§1).
  2. A large positive margin indicates a confidently classified observation. The margin mi=yixi⊤βm_i=y_i\bx_i\T\bbetami​=yi​xi⊤​β is positive exactly when example iii is correctly classified; the 0–1 loss counts errors but is discontinuous and nonconvex, so it cannot be minimized by gradient methods (§2).
  3. A smooth convex surrogate is the logistic loss. ℓlog⁡(m)=log⁡(1+e−m)\llog(m)=\log(1+e^{-m})ℓlog​(m)=log(1+e−m) is smooth, convex and decreases as the margin increases (§2, §3). Why this particular surrogate? It also arises naturally from a probabilistic model.
  4. Logistic loss = Bernoulli negative log-likelihood. With P(Y=1∣x)=σ(x⊤β)P(Y=1\mid\bx)=\sigma(\bx\T\bbeta)P(Y=1∣x)=σ(x⊤β), minimizing the average logistic loss is maximum likelihood (§3).
  5. No closed form, but a convex smooth problem. ∇F=1nX⊤(π−y~)\nabla F=\frac1n\bX\T(\bpi-\tilde\by)∇F=n1​X⊤(π−y~​), ∇2F=1nX⊤DX\nabla^2F=\frac1n\bX\T\bD\bX∇2F=n1​X⊤DX, L=∥X∥22/(4n)L=\norm{\bX}_2^2/(4n)L=∥X∥22​/(4n): gradient descent with γ≤1/L\gamma\le1/Lγ≤1/L, or Newton's method, which is IRLS (§4).

Which optimizer when?

SituationReach forWhy
Convex model, nnn moderate (say up to 10510^5105), high accuracy wantedFull-gradient methods: Newton/IRLS if ddd is small, otherwise gradient descent or quasi-Newton (L-BFGS)Few iterations, exact convergence; a full pass per iteration is affordable.
Convex model, very large nnn, good accuracy wantedSAGA, SAG or SVRGLinear convergence at the cost per step of SGD.
Very large nnn, rough accuracy is enough, or streaming dataMini-batch SGD with a decreasing step, plus averagingCheap and online; precision below the statistical error buys nothing.
Ill-conditioned problem, long narrow valleysMomentum (heavy ball or Nesterov)Builds speed along consistent directions, damps oscillations.
Gradients of very different scales across coordinates, sparse featuresAdaGrad (convex, sparse), RMSProp or Adam (nonconvex)A step size per coordinate, insensitive to gradient scale.
Deep neural networksAdam(W) or SGD with momentum, mini-batches, a learning-rate schedule (warm-up then decay)Nonconvex, huge nnn, data augmentation; variance reduction rarely pays off.

Common traps

Watch out

  1. Mixing the label conventions. Margins and log⁡(1+e−m)\log(1+e^{-m})log(1+e−m) use y∈{−1,+1}y\in\{-1,+1\}y∈{−1,+1}; the forms X⊤(π−y~)/n\bX\T(\bpi-\tilde\by)/nX⊤(π−y~​)/n and the binary cross-entropy use y~∈{0,1}\tilde y\in\{0,1\}y~​∈{0,1}, with y~=(1+y)/2\tilde y=(1+y)/2y~​=(1+y)/2.
  2. Sign of the gradient: ∇ℓi=−σ(−mi) yixi\nabla\ell_i=-\sigma(-m_i)\,y_i\bx_i∇ℓi​=−σ(−mi​)yi​xi​, with the sigmoid of minus the margin, which is the probability of the wrong label.
  3. Computing log⁡(1+e−m)\log(1+e^{-m})log(1+e−m) or ∑keuk\sum_ke^{u_k}∑k​euk​ naively: overflow for large scores. Use logaddexp and subtract the maximum score in the softmax.
  4. Assuming the logistic minimizer always exists: on separable data FFF has no minimizer and ∥w∥→∞\norm\bw\to\infty∥w∥→∞. Add a ridge penalty or stop early.
  5. Writing L=∥X∥2/(4n)L=\norm{\bX}_2/(4n)L=∥X∥2​/(4n): it is the square of the largest singular value, λmax⁡(X⊤X)/(4n)\lambda_{\max}(\bX\T\bX)/(4n)λmax​(X⊤X)/(4n).
  6. Believing that each SGD step decreases FFF. Only the conditional expectation does, and only for small enough steps.
  7. Expecting constant-step SGD to converge to β⋆\bbeta^\starβ⋆: it reaches a noise ball whose size is proportional to γ\gammaγ.
  8. Robbins–Monro with γt∝t−α\gamma_t\propto t^{-\alpha}γt​∝t−α: α=12\alpha=\tfrac12α=21​ fails ∑γt2<∞\sum\gamma_t^2<\infty∑γt2​<∞, α>1\alpha>1α>1 fails ∑γt=∞\sum\gamma_t=\infty∑γt​=∞; the admissible range is 12<α≤1\tfrac12<\alpha\le121​<α≤1.
  9. Mini-batches divide the variance by bbb, so the standard deviation only by b\sqrt bb​.
  10. Adding momentum without reducing γ\gammaγ: the effective step becomes γ/(1−θ)\gamma/(1-\theta)γ/(1−θ).
  11. Forgetting Adam's bias correction: with θ=0.9\theta=0.9θ=0.9, ρ=0.999\rho=0.999ρ=0.999 the first steps are 3 to 6.6 times too large.
  12. Treating adaptive methods as convergent with a constant step. RMSProp and Adam also need a decaying schedule to converge.
  13. Variance reduction needs a finite sum and memory (SAG/SAGA: nnn gradients, or nnn scalars for linear models); its step is set by Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​, not LLL.

Concepts

Q19Why not minimize the training error (0–1 loss) directly? Why not fit least squares to ±1\pm1±1 labels?

The 0–1 loss is piecewise constant: its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jumps, and the problem is nonconvex and combinatorial (NP-hard in general). Least squares on labels penalizes points that are classified correctly with a large margin ("too correct"), so a few easy points far from the boundary can drag it and cause errors. The logistic loss is convex, smooth, and nearly zero for large positive margins. See §2.

Q20What happens to logistic regression on linearly separable data? Give two remedies.

Scaling up any separating β\bbetaβ makes every margin larger and the loss smaller, with infimum 0 never attained: no minimizer, ∥w∥→∞\norm\bw\to\infty∥w∥→∞ along the iterations, probabilities driven to 0 and 1. Remedies: a ridge penalty λ2∥w∥2\frac\lambda2\norm\bw^22λ​∥w∥2 (strongly convex in the weights; with both classes present it has a unique, finite minimizer), or early stopping. See §4.

Q21SGD is not a descent method. Why does it still work, and what is the role of the step size in the "progress versus noise" trade-off?

Its expected progress satisfies E[F(β(t+1))∣β(t)]≤F(β(t))−γt∥∇F∥2+Lγt22E∥gt∥2\E[F(\bbeta^{(t+1)})\mid\bbeta^{(t)}]\le F(\bbeta^{(t)})-\gamma_t\norm{\nabla F}^2+\frac{L\gamma_t^2}2\E\norm{\bg_t}^2E[F(β(t+1))∣β(t)]≤F(β(t))−γt​∥∇F∥2+2Lγt2​​E∥gt​∥2: progress is first order in γt\gamma_tγt​, the noise penalty second order. Far from the solution the progress term wins; near it the gradient vanishes and only a shrinking step keeps the noise term under control. See §7.

Q22You want less noise in SGD. Compare three options: a larger mini-batch, a smaller step, variance reduction.

A batch of size bbb divides the variance by bbb at bbb times the cost per step (cheap on parallel hardware). A smaller step shrinks the noise ball proportionally but slows the initial progress; a decreasing schedule gets both, slowly. Variance reduction makes the noise vanish at the solution at the cost of memory (SAGA) or periodic full passes (SVRG), and gives linear convergence on strongly convex finite sums.

Q23Explain "there is no universally best optimizer" with two contrasting situations.

A convex logistic regression on 10410^4104 examples where you need an accurate solution: Newton/IRLS or SAGA reach machine precision quickly, and constant-step Adam would only hover around the optimum. A deep network on millions of augmented images: no finite sum to exploit, nonconvex landscape, moderate accuracy needed; mini-batch SGD with momentum or Adam with a schedule is the practical choice, and full-gradient or variance-reduced methods waste computation.
